events.title: The Tuathaich homeland fixed
events.body: The descendants of the humans stranded by the Severance are settled by law in the north of the island and held there. It is a confinement; yet their children's children call it home.

events.title: The Hale household lodged at Caol mhòr
events.body: Walter Hale comes north with his wife Ellen and their children David and Alice among the households the guard walks into the homeland that summer, and is given a loft over a net-store on the harbour street at Caol mhòr, his for as long as nobody wants it back.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The Tuathaich homeland fixed

told_in.book: Of the Stones on the North Roads
told_in.section: I. Of the Quay at Caol mhòr

events.title: Hale takes to copying the Caol mhòr harbour slate
events.body: With no office and no book of his own, Walter Hale begins copying the catch weighed at the Caol mhòr quay from the fishermen's slate before it is rubbed clean each evening, the first written record the harbour keeps of itself under the new homeland.

links.label: At the same time
links.title: The boundary stones set

told_in.book: Of the Stones on the North Roads
told_in.section: I. Of the Quay at Caol mhòr

events.title: The north's first harvest falls short
events.body: Sown late on ground half the settled households have never worked, the Tuathaich shires' first harvest comes in thin, short in the straw and light in the ear, while the stores that once came over the water from an Tìr Thall do not come again.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The hungry year at Doire ghlas

told_in.book: Of the Stones on the North Roads
told_in.section: III. Of the Thin Harvest

events.title: The Caol mhòr catch shared by households
events.body: As the herring run late and thin that autumn, the Caol mhòr boats stop selling their catch to whoever comes first to the quay and begin sharing it out by households instead, a change no minute records and every household in the town keeps to.

links.label: At the same time
links.title: The hungry year at Doire ghlas

told_in.book: Of the Stones on the North Roads
told_in.section: III. Of the Thin Harvest

events.title: The Severance companies stood down
events.body: The war-companies of the last campaign against the human administration are disbanded at Cathair dhearg. Their rolls go to the council unburned, and the companies are never abolished; they live on as names on a list.

links.title: The Grey House among the old companies

events.title: Fearchar mac Raghnaill's plea that his company's roll be kept
events.body: At the muster in Cathair dhearg's drill-yard, Captain Fearchar mac Raghnaill asks neither for pay nor for arms but that the roll of his company's names not be burned with the loose paper of the stand-down, since every name on it stood where the roll says he stood.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The Severance companies stood down

told_in.book: Of the Winter of the Severance
told_in.section: IV. Of Cathair dhearg and the Rolls

events.title: The disbanded companies' rolls kept, not burned
events.body: On a clerk's asking, the master of the chests orders that the rolls of the stood-down war-companies be kept and boxed rather than burned with the rest of the muster's loose paper; Fearchar mac Raghnaill's roll is the first spared, though he never learns it.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The Severance companies stood down

told_in.book: Of the Winter of the Severance
told_in.section: IV. Of Cathair dhearg and the Rolls

events.title: Ailean's list of the chests begun
events.body: Carrying sixty-one companies' rolls down into the council's vault, Ailean mac Iain keeps, unasked, a written list of which roll went into which chest and in what order, the first record of its kind the council's vault has ever had.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The Severance companies stood down

told_in.book: Of the Winter of the Severance
told_in.section: IV. Of Cathair dhearg and the Rolls

events.title: The war-vault sealed at Cathair dhearg
events.body: The council's vault of war papers is closed and bricked over at Cathair dhearg, the seal meant to stand until some later year gives cause to break it; the master of the chests signs Ailean mac Iain's list of the vault's contents before it is filed.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The Severance companies stood down

told_in.book: Of the Winter of the Severance
told_in.section: V. Of the Chests Locked

events.title: The boundary stones set
events.body: Stones are set on the north roads where the Tuathaich country begins. No wall follows them. Many stand by the roadside yet, and no one has been paid to move them.

links.label: Caused by
links.title: The surveyors cross the boundary stones

links.label: At the same time
links.title: Hale takes to copying the Caol mhòr harbour slate

links.title: The boundary stone set on the Caol mhòr road

links.label: Leads to

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The old woman at the farm gate

events.title: The boundary stone set on the Caol mhòr road
events.body: The council's masons set a stone where the drove path crosses the road out of Caol mhòr, cut in Dia-thìris and left without a wall to follow it. Walter Hale walks out with his son David to read what neither of them can make out.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The boundary stones set

told_in.book: Of the Stones on the North Roads
told_in.section: II. Of the Stone on the Caol mhòr Road

events.title: The hungry year at Doire ghlas
events.body: The stores that came over the water from an Tìr Thall come no more, and in their first year alone the northern settlements go short of grain. Tuathaich memory puts the dead at Doire ghlas above two hundred. The Dia-thìrich made no count.

links.title: The north's first harvest falls short

events.title: The guard posted at the heads of the north roads
events.body: The council sets a guard-post on every road running north out of the settled country, a captain and a dozen men at each, to hold the line the columns had walked in winter and to turn back any who wander south of it.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The Tuathaich homeland fixed

told_in.book: Of the Winter of the Severance
told_in.section: II. Of the Guard at the Heads of the Roads

events.title: Ailean mac Iain rides as tally-clerk to the guard
events.body: A young clerk of the council's service is sent to ride between the new guard-posts with a book, counting who passes north, who turns back, and who is too sick to walk, so that the council should have some record of the settling beyond the guard's own word.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The Tuathaich homeland fixed

told_in.book: Of the Winter of the Severance
told_in.section: II. Of the Guard at the Heads of the Roads

events.title: The last column counted through at the Caol mhòr road
events.body: Forty-one souls are counted through the guard-post on the Caol mhòr road, the last column of the winter's walking, two dying before evening; after them the road stands empty, and the tally-clerk's book records no further column that year.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The Tuathaich homeland fixed

told_in.book: Of the Winter of the Severance
told_in.section: II. Of the Guard at the Heads of the Roads

events.title: The council's word on the homeland read at Caol mhòr
events.body: The council's law fixing Tìr-dhùthchais nan Tuathach in the north is read from the steps of the harbour-house at Caol mhòr before a wet crowd, first in Dia-thìris, then, by the council's own order, in the humans' tongue for those who have no other.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The Tuathaich homeland fixed

told_in.book: Of the Winter of the Severance
told_in.section: III. Of Caol mhòr and the Two Words

events.title: Walter Hale found to read the council's word into the humans' tongue
events.body: Walter Hale, once a harbour clerk of Ros bheag, is fetched from the crowd at Caol mhòr to render the council's proclamation into the humans' tongue, and reads it plainly, without the first reader's polish, to a crowd that takes it in near silence.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The Tuathaich homeland fixed

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The Moot at Caol mhòr

told_in.book: Of the Winter of the Severance
told_in.section: III. Of Caol mhòr and the Two Words

events.title: Hale's correction entered in a clerk's margin
events.body: Asked how his rendering of the council's word differed from the paper he was given, Hale tells Ailean mac Iain that the truer word for what was done to the north was not "settled" but "held"; Ailean writes the two words in the margin of his own copy, unasked.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The Tuathaich homeland fixed

told_in.book: Of the Winter of the Severance
told_in.section: III. Of Caol mhòr and the Two Words

events.title: The humans' chapel at Ros bheag shut for good
events.body: Word reaches Caol mhòr that the humans' chapel at Ros bheag, shut since An t-Aiseag closed, is to be shut for good on the council's order; Walter Hale, once the town's harbour clerk, brings the news to Ailean mac Iain without asking anything of him.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The hungry year at Doire ghlas

told_in.book: Of the Winter of the Severance
told_in.section: III. Of Caol mhòr and the Two Words

events.title: The Ros bheag bell carted north
events.body: The council's men take down the bell of the shut chapel at Ros bheag and cart it away roped in sacking, bound, it is said, for wherever in the north the humans' faith may still be kept; Ailean mac Iain sees the cart pass and notes it without comment.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The hungry year at Doire ghlas

told_in.book: Of the Winter of the Severance
told_in.section: III. Of Caol mhòr and the Two Words

events.title: The companies wait on their packs in the market square
events.body: In the first week of an t-Ògmhios the market square of Cathair dhearg, a place of stalls and cattle before the war, is given over to the companies of Cogadh nam Beann waiting their turn to be stood down, sitting on their packs in the sun with only the paperwork of the war left to them.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The Severance companies stood down

told_in.book: Of the Winter of the Severance
told_in.section: IV. Of Cathair dhearg and the Rolls

events.title: The master of the chests signs beneath Ailean's list
events.body: The master of the chests reads Ailean mac Iain's four sheets by lamplight at the foot of the vault stair, signs his own name beneath Ailean's on the last of them more from courtesy than conviction, and carries them up to be filed before the door is bricked shut.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The Severance companies stood down

told_in.book: Of the Winter of the Severance
told_in.section: V. Of the Chests Locked

events.title: An old captain's word at the guard fire
events.body: Griogair, an old captain of the guard at the heads of the north roads who had lost two fingers to a humans' picket, tells Ailean mac Iain over a fire that a line held by soldiers is only a line waiting for the soldiers to be needed elsewhere; Ailean writes it in the back pages he keeps for himself.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The boundary stones set

told_in.book: Of the Winter of the Severance
told_in.section: II. Of the Guard at the Heads of the Roads

events.title: The old woman at the farm gate
events.body: A half-day short of the first guard-post an old woman asks Ailean mac Iain at her gate whether the boy who once kept her sheep will be let come back for them now the fighting is done; he tells her truthfully that he does not know, and writes nothing of it, since it fits none of his columns.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The boundary stones set

told_in.book: Of the Winter of the Severance
told_in.section: II. Of the Guard at the Heads of the Roads

events.title: Meal carried from Caol mhòr to Doire ghlas
events.body: The householders of Caol mhòr send three cartloads of oats and salt fish ten miles inland to Doire ghlas in the depth of the hungry winter, and Walter Hale walks with them, carrying the town's meal and, unlooked for, its grief.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The hungry year at Doire ghlas

told_in.book: Of the Stones on the North Roads
told_in.section: IV. Of the Meal Carried to Doire ghlas

events.title: The graves on the rise above Doire ghlas
events.body: Above ten dead of the hungry winter, children among them, are buried in shallow graves on the rise above Doire ghlas, dug close together in half-frozen ground; the earliest of the winter's dead had already been buried singly, unrecorded, before the town thought to keep any count.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The hungry year at Doire ghlas

told_in.book: Of the Stones on the North Roads
told_in.section: IV. Of the Meal Carried to Doire ghlas

events.title: Walter Hale's day-book begun
events.body: Home from Doire ghlas, Walter Hale buys a fishmonger's ledger and writes the town's name and a number in it by lamplight, the first line of a private accounting of A' Bhliadhna Acrach's dead that no council south of the guard-stone has asked for or knows exists.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The hungry year at Doire ghlas

told_in.book: Of the Stones on the North Roads
told_in.section: V. Of the Book Begun

events.title: Seed oats taken from the Doire mhin mill on credit
events.body: With the hungry winter not yet spent, the Tuathaich shires take seed oats from the mill at Doire mhin on credit against the coming harvest, the first debt of its kind the north carries into the new kingdom's account books.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The hungry year at Doire ghlas

told_in.book: Of the Stones on the North Roads
told_in.section: IV. Of the Meal Carried to Doire ghlas

events.title: The names pinned in the Doire ghlas church porch
events.body: In the first mild week of spring a woman of the parish goes house to house through Doire ghlas gathering the names of A' Bhliadhna Acrach's dead, and pins them, above fifteen strips of paper in a dozen hands, along the boards of the church porch, where the town comes to call it the porch of the names.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The hungry year at Doire ghlas

told_in.book: Of the Stones on the North Roads
told_in.section: VI. Of the Names in the Porch

events.title: Walter Hale reads the porch of the names
events.body: Walter Hale walks the ten miles to Doire ghlas a second time to read the names pinned in the church porch, and copies every one into a second book begun that winter, keeping the town's own count beside his, though neither squares exactly with the other.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The hungry year at Doire ghlas

told_in.book: Of the Stones on the North Roads
told_in.section: VI. Of the Names in the Porch

events.title: The herring return to the Caol mhòr grounds
events.body: By the second spring the herring come back to the Caol mhòr grounds in numbers not seen since before An Dealachadh, and the town, having taken nothing from the sea that winter that it did not share, takes the shoals as the sea's answer.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The hungry year at Doire ghlas

told_in.book: Of the Stones on the North Roads
told_in.section: VI. Of the Names in the Porch

events.title: The Widow Fenn's two fish
events.body: Ellen Hale comes home from the Caol mhòr quay in the first week of an Dàmhair and tells her husband that Peg Carrick's mother has given the Widow Fenn, who has no boat, two fish out of a catch of nine; it is the first word of the sharing Tional nan Tuathach later counts its first work.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The hungry year at Doire ghlas

told_in.book: Of the Stones on the North Roads
told_in.section: III. Of the Thin Harvest

events.title: The human counting-houses emptied
events.body: Clerks of the council enter the human administration's counting-houses at Cathair dhearg, Ros dhomhain and Seann Skell and carry off every written thing. What the raids of the war have left of the tithe ledgers is boxed with the rest, unread, for few of the clerks can read the humans' hand.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Ailean set to the counting-house at Cathair dhearg

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The fire-damaged tithe rolls boxed as loose leaves

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The Ros dhomhain tariff copied into Dia-thìris

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The district surveys found behind a locked grating

links.label: Caused by
links.title: The surveys boxed apart and labelled for the council

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The humans' ledgers boxed unread

events.title: Ailean set to the counting-house at Cathair dhearg
events.body: Ailean mac Iain is set to the humans' counting-house at Cathair dhearg to box the north wall's tithe rolls unread, and says nothing of the letters a Mission reader taught him as a boy, for a clerk who reads aloud what he is told only to box is not a clerk kept long.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The human counting-houses emptied

told_in.book: Of the Counting-Houses and the Broken Locks
told_in.section: I. Of the Boxes at Cathair dhearg

events.title: The fire-damaged tithe rolls boxed as loose leaves
events.body: Where the counting-house fire at Cathair dhearg burned a shelf's ledgers through the middle rather than whole, Ailean gathers the crumbling leaves as best their order can be guessed and marks the crate that the order is his own guess and not to be trusted past that.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The human counting-houses emptied

told_in.book: Of the Counting-Houses and the Broken Locks
told_in.section: I. Of the Boxes at Cathair dhearg

events.title: The Ros dhomhain tariff copied into Dia-thìris
events.body: At the harbour offices of Ros dhomhain, Ailean copies the humans' tariff tables clause by clause into Dia-thìris, building the words for duties his own tongue had never before had cause to name, and the duty itself stands unchanged under its new ink.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The human counting-houses emptied

told_in.book: Of the Counting-Houses and the Broken Locks
told_in.section: II. Of Ros dhomhain's Sheds

events.title: The district surveys found behind a locked grating
events.body: In the whole counting-house at Seann Skell in the west, Ailean forces a locked grating and finds eleven rolled district surveys, the only whole survey of the island's fields anywhere to be had, each walked, measured and scaled by the humans' own hand.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The human counting-houses emptied

told_in.book: Of the Counting-Houses and the Broken Locks
told_in.section: III. Of the Labelled Box

events.title: The surveys boxed apart and labelled for the council
events.body: Ruairidh orders the district surveys boxed apart from the tithe rolls, for the council's own clerks rather than the reckoners, and Ailean chalks the crate's lid with six words rather than a description: the shires will be drawn on them.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The human counting-houses emptied

told_in.book: Of the Counting-Houses and the Broken Locks
told_in.section: III. Of the Labelled Box

events.title: The state's seal begun at Cathair dhearg
events.body: In the same week as the proclamation, the council's engraver at Cathair dhearg begins cutting a seal for the state's own letters, to be set upon documents no different in kind from the ones Ailean spent the summer boxing unread.

links.label: At the same time
links.title: Rìoghachd Dia-thìr declared

told_in.book: Of the Counting-Houses and the Broken Locks
told_in.section: V. Of the Proclamation

events.title: The north-west ports without a master
events.body: At Ceann mhòr, Cathair gheal and Inis àrsaidh the humans' harbour officers had sailed with the last ships before the crossing closed, and taken their keys with them. The Tuathaich fishermen break the locks of the harbour stores and share out what they find, house by house.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The harbour store's lock broken at Ceann mhòr

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The unfished nets loosed at Cathair gheal

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The reckoning drawn up by three women of Inis àrsaidh

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The north-west locks left unanswered

events.title: The harbour store's lock broken at Ceann mhòr
events.body: A fisherman of Ceann mhòr breaks the lock of the humans' harbour store with a hammer and stands back to let the town see what is inside, and it is the town, not the man who struck the lock, that shares the rope, canvas and salt out house by house within the hour.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The north-west ports without a master

told_in.book: Of the Counting-Houses and the Broken Locks
told_in.section: IV. Of What the North Tells

events.title: The unfished nets loosed at Cathair gheal
events.body: A whole loft of nets that had never been fished goes out to every boat in the harbour at Cathair gheal on a single tide, and the fleet fishes that year with gear it never paid a coin for and never afterward wonders whose it had been.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The north-west ports without a master

told_in.book: Of the Counting-Houses and the Broken Locks
told_in.section: IV. Of What the North Tells

events.title: The reckoning drawn up by three women of Inis àrsaidh
events.body: At Inis àrsaidh, poorer and smaller than its neighbours, three women of the town draw up on the spot the reckoning of who has a boat and who has none, and so who needs rope or salt the more, with no office to do it and none afterward to say they did it wrong.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The north-west ports without a master

told_in.book: Of the Counting-Houses and the Broken Locks
told_in.section: IV. Of What the North Tells

events.title: The north-west locks left unanswered
events.body: No maor comes north to ask who struck the first lock at Ceann mhòr, Cathair gheal or Inis àrsaidh before the following spring, by which time there is nothing left locked to account for, and the towns' own telling of the broken stores hardens into the kind of story a place keeps because it likes its shape.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The north-west ports without a master

told_in.book: Of the Counting-Houses and the Broken Locks
told_in.section: IV. Of What the North Tells

events.title: Rìoghachd Dia-thìr declared
events.body: The state names itself a kingdom, though it is ruled as before. Its own records carry the same contradiction to this day.

links.label: At the same time
links.title: The state's seal begun at Cathair dhearg

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Rìoghachd Dia-thìr proclaimed from the counting-house steps

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The proclamation read at the market crosses of the south

events.title: Rìoghachd Dia-thìr proclaimed from the counting-house steps
events.body: A herald reads the council's proclamation from the steps of the Cathair dhearg counting-house, naming the state Rìoghachd Dia-thìr and the years of settling complete; Ailean stands in the crowd and does not cheer, thinking the naming a kind of label, true as far as it goes and silent about the rest.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Rìoghachd Dia-thìr declared

told_in.book: Of the Counting-Houses and the Broken Locks
told_in.section: V. Of the Proclamation

events.title: The proclamation read at the market crosses of the south
events.body: Copies of the proclamation styling the state Rìoghachd Dia-thìr are read at the market crosses of every southern town within the fortnight, in the same flat, official voice, whatever crowd happens to be standing near enough to hear it.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Rìoghachd Dia-thìr declared

told_in.book: Of the Counting-Houses and the Broken Locks
told_in.section: V. Of the Proclamation

events.title: The humans' ledgers boxed unread
events.body: Ruairidh, master of the counting-house room at Cathair dhearg, gives Ailean mac Iain the whole northern wall of the humans' ledgers to clear and tells him to box them unread; Ailean, who could have read several of them, boxes them as he is told.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The human counting-houses emptied

told_in.book: Of the Counting-Houses and the Broken Locks
told_in.section: I. Of the Boxes at Cathair dhearg

events.title: The Moot at Caol mhòr
events.body: Tuathaich householders of the northern towns meet at Caol mhòr and choose for their speaker Walter Hale, once a harbour clerk. The Moot has no standing in Dia-thìrich law. It meets all the same and keeps its own minutes, which run unbroken from that day to this.

links.label: Caused by
links.title: Martha Greaves's first sitting as speaker

links.label: Caused by
links.title: Walter Hale's harbour ledger

links.label: Caused by
links.title: The rebound set laid in the press at Caol mhòr

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Walter Hale found to read the council's word into the humans' tongue

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Tional nan Tuathach votes its first winter measures

links.title: The Doire ghlas dead voted into Tional nan Tuathach's record

links.title: The granary founded at Caol mhòr

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The gathering of northern households takes the name Moot

events.title: The council of the kingdom seated
events.body: A royal council of twelve is seated at Cathair dhearg, drawn from the custodian families and the captains of the Severance war. Its minute-books are the oldest unbroken record of the state in this age.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Tional nan Tuathach's letter received and filed

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Ailean mac Iain and Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill sworn under-clerks

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Comhairle na Rìoghachd seated and its chairs filled

links.label: Leads to
links.title: A councillor asks what a Moot is

events.title: Tional nan Tuathach votes its first winter measures
events.body: The households gathered at Caol mhòr vote, in the same sitting that opens Tional nan Tuathach's book, to lay by grain against the coming winter and to keep watch on the north roads, having buried too many of their own the winter before to trust the season a second time unwarned.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The Moot at Caol mhòr

told_in.book: Of the Moot and the Council of Twelve
told_in.section: II. Of the Book with Nothing in It

events.title: The Doire ghlas dead voted into Tional nan Tuathach's record
events.body: Walter Hale tells the gathered households what he counted on the rise above Doire ghlas and what the church porch's names afterward told him, and Tional nan Tuathach votes, without a voice raised against it, that the count stand as the north's own record of that winter's dead.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The hungry year at Doire ghlas

links.label: At the same time
links.title: The Moot at Caol mhòr

told_in.book: Of the Moot and the Council of Twelve
told_in.section: II. Of the Book with Nothing in It

events.title: The granary founded at Caol mhòr
events.body: Tional nan Tuathach sets a common store under lock in the harbour-house cellar, each household to give what it can spare, and names three keepers answerable for it: a harbour man trusted with a scale, a smith of Doire ghlas, and a widow of A' Bhliadhna Acrach who had buried two children in it.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The Moot at Caol mhòr

told_in.book: Of the Moot and the Council of Twelve
told_in.section: II. Of the Book with Nothing in It

events.title: Tional nan Tuathach's letter drafted for the council
events.body: Walter Hale drafts, and Tional nan Tuathach amends and approves, four careful lines telling the council at Cathair dhearg of the households met at Caol mhòr and of a winter's dead the north had buried and counted without the south's knowledge, asking nothing beyond that the fact be noted.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The Moot at Caol mhòr

told_in.book: Of the Moot and the Council of Twelve
told_in.section: III. Of the Letter South

events.title: Robert Carrick carries Tional nan Tuathach's letter south
events.body: Peg Carrick's younger brother Robert, fifteen and never before further from Caol mhòr than Doire ghlas, a carter, carries the letter south to Cathair dhearg with it sewn into the lining of his coat, and is the better part of a fortnight on a road he does not know.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The Moot at Caol mhòr

told_in.book: Of the Moot and the Council of Twelve
told_in.section: III. Of the Letter South

events.title: Tional nan Tuathach's letter received and filed
events.body: A clerk at the harbour-house in Cathair dhearg takes Tional nan Tuathach's letter from Robert Carrick's hand, tells him it will be seen to, and sends him home with no answer; the disposal, once the letter reaches the council chamber, is three words in the state's own minute-book.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The council of the kingdom seated

told_in.book: Of the Moot and the Council of Twelve
told_in.section: IV. Of the Twelve at Cathair dhearg

events.title: Ailean mac Iain and Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill sworn under-clerks
events.body: On the twenty-third of an t-Sultain the council's newest under-clerks are sworn on the custodians' worn oath-book, Ailean mac Iain among them and, beside him, Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill, a council clerk's daughter of the capital who has wanted the office since she was old enough to know what a minute-book was for.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The council of the kingdom seated

told_in.book: Of the Moot and the Council of Twelve
told_in.section: IV. Of the Twelve at Cathair dhearg

events.title: Comhairle na Rìoghachd seated and its chairs filled
events.body: Twelve chairs are filled at Cathair dhearg, drawn from the custodian families and the captains of Cogadh nam Beann: among them Fearchar mac Raghnaill, whose company's roll was kept the summer before; Beathag nic Artair of the old custodian houses; Griogair mac Tormoid of the western shore; and Cailean mac Sheumais, who commanded a company at the fords of the western hills.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The council of the kingdom seated

told_in.book: Of the Moot and the Council of Twelve
told_in.section: IV. Of the Twelve at Cathair dhearg

events.title: A councillor asks what a Moot is
events.body: When Tional nan Tuathach's letter is read before the twelve, Cailean mac Sheumais asks plainly what a Moot is; no one in the chamber can answer with any certainty beyond Fearchar mac Raghnaill's memory of the word from a harbour clerk at Caol mhòr, and the letter is moved to be filed.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The council of the kingdom seated

told_in.book: Of the Moot and the Council of Twelve
told_in.section: IV. Of the Twelve at Cathair dhearg

events.title: The gathering of northern households takes the name Moot
events.body: In the weeks after its first sitting the gathering of the north's households comes, without a vote taken on it, to be called Tional nan Tuathach, a word one of its own pursers remembered from an old book of the humans' law, half in earnest and half against themselves.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The Moot at Caol mhòr

told_in.book: Of the Moot and the Council of Twelve
told_in.section: I. Of the Long Room at Caol mhòr

events.title: Robert Carrick comes home with an empty satchel
events.body: Robert Carrick comes back to Caol mhòr on a wet evening in the first week of an Dàmhair with an empty satchel and one report: Tional nan Tuathach's letter was handed at the harbour-house in Cathair dhearg to a clerk who told him word would be sent back in time, and did not look at him.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The Moot at Caol mhòr

told_in.book: Of the Moot and the Council of Twelve
told_in.section: III. Of the Letter South

events.title: Ailean sent to the Ros dhomhain sheds
events.body: A month after his swearing, Ailean mac Iain is sent from Cathair dhearg to Ros dhomhain to help Dùghall mac Iain turn the humans' tariff into Dia-thìris, line by line, since the harbour cannot wait for a tariff written fresh.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The harbour-houses of Ros dhomhain taken over

told_in.book: Of the Grey Water and the Crowning
told_in.section: I. Of the Sheds at Ros dhomhain

events.title: Dùghall mac Iain's reason for copying, not writing anew
events.body: Dùghall mac Iain tells Ailean he keeps the humans' sums and changes only the words, since a skipper who has long paid a known tariff pays it gladly to a new hand, and a tariff written fresh would only be cheated the more freely for its newness.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The harbour-houses of Ros dhomhain taken over

told_in.book: Of the Grey Water and the Crowning
told_in.section: I. Of the Sheds at Ros dhomhain

events.title: Ailean's private book begun
events.body: At Ros dhomhain, Ailean begins a private book of his own, bound in undyed leather, in which he sets beside his day's plain clerking the things said to him that seem worth keeping, though he does not yet know their use.

links.label: At the same time
links.title: The harbour-houses of Ros dhomhain taken over

told_in.book: Of the Grey Water and the Crowning
told_in.section: I. Of the Sheds at Ros dhomhain

events.title: The harbour-houses of Ros dhomhain taken over
events.body: The customs sheds that the humans built at Ros dhomhain, the greatest port of the kingdom, pass to Dia-thìrich harbour-masters. The first of them, Dùghall mac Iain, keeps the humans' tariff for want of another, and in the years after puts it into Dia-thìris line by line.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Ailean sent to the Ros dhomhain sheds

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Dùghall mac Iain's reason for copying, not writing anew

links.label: At the same time
links.title: Ailean's private book begun

events.title: The ship sent north
events.body: The council sends a ship out past the north-western capes and north-about to seek the crossing the humans used. She returns after a month of grey water with nothing to tell: no land, no ship, no sign of the passage. No second ship is sent. The priests of Manannan at Seann Skell say that the lord of the sea has shut the eastern sea again, as they have prayed him to since the Crossing.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Ailean named tally-clerk for An Sireadh

links.label: Leads to
links.title: An Sireadh's log kept and filed

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Aonghas mac Mhurchaidh turns the ship for home

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The prayer said over An Sireadh's return

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Nine days of mist on the grey water

links.label: Leads to
links.title: An Sireadh careened for the winter at Seann Skell

events.title: Niall crowned
events.body: Niall, first ruler of the restored kingdom, takes the throne at Cathair dhearg by Macha's rite. His is the first name in the line that the state's chronicles keep unbroken from this year on.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Ailean learns of the crowning at Seann Skell

events.title: A saying enters speech
events.body: The crowning passes with so little dispute that 'mar a thàinig Niall', the way Niall came, becomes a saying for any smooth handing-on of power. It is first found written in a tavern ledger at Cathair dhearg, against a debt settled without argument.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Ailean learns of the crowning at Seann Skell

events.title: The shires drawn
events.body: The council divides the kingdom into siorrachdan, each named for its seat, and keeps most of the human administration's district lines under the new names. The humans' surveys are the only whole ones on the island; the kingdom uses them and says nothing of it.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The shire map drawn from the humans' survey

events.title: The windy coast left out
events.body: The shire lines stop where the humans' survey stopped, at the edge of the great moss of the far north-west. The windy coast beyond, an Oirthir Ghaothach, with its sealers and fowlers, is set in no shire and given no maor. The council's minute says only that it 'is not in the survey'.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The minute that an Oirthir Ghaothach is not in the survey

events.title: The island shires
events.body: Two rocks that each kept a customs station of the Administration, Eilean dhìreach off the Tuathaich coast and Eilean ìseal off the east coast, are kept as shires of their own, for the council has no rule for folding one district into its neighbour. Neither has a town to name it, and each shire takes the name of its island.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The two island shires entered on the map

events.title: The market of Ceann mhòr
events.body: At the drawing of the shires the Tuathaich of Ceann mhòr are granted a market right for the north-west coast. Its court sits in the harbour store whose locks the fishermen broke. Fish, whale-oil, seal-oil, amber, dyes and the tobacco of the concession farms are sold there.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Ceann mhòr's market right entered on the map

events.title: Ailean named tally-clerk for An Sireadh
events.body: The council names Ailean mac Iain tally-clerk for the ship sent north-about to seek An t-Aiseag, and he rides hard for Cuan shean to be aboard by the sailing day, leaving the Ros dhomhain tariff a third finished.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The ship sent north

told_in.book: Of the Grey Water and the Crowning
told_in.section: II. Of the Grey Water

events.title: An Sireadh's log kept and filed
events.body: Ailean keeps An Sireadh's log the length of her voyage, heading, wind and soundings set down plainly through a month of grey water and mist, and the finished log is filed with the council on her return.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The ship sent north

told_in.book: Of the Grey Water and the Crowning
told_in.section: II. Of the Grey Water

events.title: Aonghas mac Mhurchaidh turns the ship for home
events.body: Sixteen days out with the stores a third gone, Aonghas mac Mhurchaidh orders An Sireadh about, telling Ailean the sea has not been found empty so much as it has refused, this once, to show itself.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The ship sent north

told_in.book: Of the Grey Water and the Crowning
told_in.section: II. Of the Grey Water

events.title: The prayer said over An Sireadh's return
events.body: The priests of Manannan come down to the quay at Seann Skell in the west as An Sireadh makes her berth and say again the old prayer that the sea be kept shut, said first at her going and now at her coming home empty-handed.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The ship sent north

told_in.book: Of the Grey Water and the Crowning
told_in.section: III. Of the Way Niall Came

events.title: Ailean learns of the crowning at Seann Skell
events.body: Home after a month at sea, Ailean learns of Niall's crowning from an innkeeper near the harbour at Seann Skell in the west, and writes the day into his private book with nothing beside it, having seen nothing of it with his own eyes.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: A saying enters speech

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Niall crowned

told_in.book: Of the Grey Water and the Crowning
told_in.section: III. Of the Way Niall Came

events.title: The shire map drawn from the humans' survey
events.body: Through an Dùbhlachd, Ailean copies the humans' district survey onto a fresh sheet and sets the Dia-thìris names of the shires against it, for the council to show the twelve without embarrassment at governing by a stranger's paperwork.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The shires drawn

told_in.book: Of the Grey Water and the Crowning
told_in.section: IV. Of the Edge of the Map

events.title: The minute that an Oirthir Ghaothach is not in the survey
events.body: Where the humans' survey ends unmarked at the great moss, Ailean writes a single short line rather than leave the gap unexplained: that an Oirthir Ghaothach is not in the survey, a line the council's copying afterward carries to every maor's court unremarked.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The windy coast left out

told_in.book: Of the Grey Water and the Crowning
told_in.section: IV. Of the Edge of the Map

events.title: The two island shires entered on the map
events.body: Finding no council rule for folding a small holding into its neighbour, Ailean enters the two customs-station rocks as shires of their own, each taking the name of the island it sits on and noted as holding no town.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The island shires

told_in.book: Of the Grey Water and the Crowning
told_in.section: IV. Of the Edge of the Map

events.title: Ceann mhòr's market right entered on the map
events.body: The council grants the Ceann mhòr fishermen a market right for their two years' rough trading in the broken-locked harbour store, and Ailean sets the grant down as the smallest clause on the whole map, the one thing on it the townsfolk had already made true for themselves.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The market of Ceann mhòr

told_in.book: Of the Grey Water and the Crowning
told_in.section: IV. Of the Edge of the Map

events.title: Nine days of mist on the grey water
events.body: For nine days running An Sireadh sails north-about in mist so thick the bow cannot always be seen from the wheel, under short sail with a man forward and a horn; twice the lookout swears to a low dark shape off the starboard bow, and twice it is not there when she stands in toward it.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The ship sent north

told_in.book: Of the Grey Water and the Crowning
told_in.section: II. Of the Grey Water

events.title: An Sireadh careened for the winter at Seann Skell
events.body: An Sireadh is laid up for the winter at Seann Skell in the west, careened and her hull scraped bare of a month's weed, the council having no second voyage in mind for her.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The ship sent north

told_in.book: Of the Grey Water and the Crowning
told_in.section: IV. Of the Edge of the Map

events.title: The maoir appointed
events.body: A maor is set over each shire to gather the Crown's dues and keep its peace. In the Tuathaich shires the maoir are Dia-thìrich, lodged in the seat towns. At Ceann mhòr the maor lives in the old human magistrate's house, and the townsfolk call it by its old name.

events.title: The Crown's dues set
events.body: The council sets the dues the maoir shall gather: a head-due, cìs-cinn, on every household by the number of its heads, and a market-due, cìs-margaidh, on every sale made by a seller of the kingdom. The humans' harbour tariff at Ros dhomhain stands until the kingdom has a coin of its own to take the market-due in.

events.title: The roll of arms
events.body: The council's clerks make Clàr nan Suaicheantas, a roll of arms, so that each maor may seal the letters of his court. The kingdom's arms are cut anew from the old seal of the custody, and every shire is given arms of its own. Many charges are copied from a book of arms left at the Residency, and so lions, parrots and crocodiles stand on the seals of shires where none was ever seen. The Dia-thìrich shires bear the pointed shield of the custody's seal; the Tuathaich shires keep the rounded shield of the humans' district seals. At Seann Skell in the west the house of Òrd Mhanannain asks for its badge, the yellow scorpion of Manannan's cup, and that shire alone of all the roll bears a scorpion.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The first maor's seal cut from Clàr nan Suaicheantas

links.label: Leads to
links.title: A hill shire questions its new arms

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Tòmas draws Clàr nan Suaicheantas

events.title: The maor of Baile Mòr mhòr
events.body: Coinneach mac Ailein, first maor of Siorrachd Baile Mòr mhòr, holds his court under the market roof of the town, for the humans' courthouse has burned. He keeps it there after the new courthouse is built, and so do those who follow him.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Coinneach mac Ailein settles the fishwives' stall-place

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Coinneach mac Ailein moves his court back under the market roof

events.title: Tonn Mhòr Cnoc chaol
events.body: The Great Wave falls without warning on the southern coast and lays waste Cnoc chaol, Cuan dhearg and Achadh mhin in a single night. It is the first disaster the new state meets by its own means.

links.label: Caused by
links.title: The council votes a relief party for the southern coast

events.title: The dead of the Great Wave counted
events.body: Relief parties from Cathair dhearg come to Cuan dhearg on the southern coast and count the dead of the three settlements at a little over forty. The harbour of Cuan dhearg is gone, and its boats are found in the fields behind the town. The wave has run on up the gulf as far as Ros gharbh, the seat of its shire, broken its quays and cast the gulf's fishing fleet on the headland. The town stands high and loses few of its people, but nearly every boat.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The council votes a relief party for the southern coast

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Ailean's tally-book of the wave begun

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The dead of Cuan dhearg buried on the rise

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The boats left standing in the barley

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Ros gharbh's fleet counted on the headland

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Ros gharbh's boats rebuilt

events.title: Achadh mhin under salt
events.body: The fields of Achadh mhin lie under salt and will not bear. The council moves the survivors to higher ground and pays for their seed from the treasury. It is the first relief the restored kingdom grants.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The treasury's first relief roll voted

events.title: Cnoc chaol rebuilt on the hill
events.body: Cnoc chaol is built again on the slope behind the old town, beyond the wave's reach. The old site is left as the water left it. The townsfolk call it an Tràigh Bhàthte, the drowned strand, and do not build there.

events.title: The first maor's seal cut from Clàr nan Suaicheantas
events.body: The council's clerk Tòmas cuts the first working seal from Clàr nan Suaicheantas, the newly drawn roll of arms, for a maor of the south-west to press upon his letters; the shire's borrowed lion goes out sealing writs before the ink of the roll itself is fully dry.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The roll of arms

told_in.section: I. Of the Maoir and the Roll of Arms

events.title: Coinneach mac Ailein settles the fishwives' stall-place
events.body: In his first sitting under the market roof at Baile Mòr mhòr, the new maor Coinneach mac Ailein settles a two-year quarrel over a stall-place by asking the gathered stallholders for the truth of it rather than ruling from the bench alone, and takes their answer as his judgment.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The maor of Baile Mòr mhòr

told_in.section: I. Of the Maoir and the Roll of Arms

events.title: The council votes a relief party for the southern coast
events.body: Before its morning sitting breaks, Comhairle na Rìoghachd votes grain, blankets, timber and men down the coast road to Cuan dhearg, and orders a tally kept of what is found, the first time the twelve have met before full light since An Dealachadh itself.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Tonn Mhòr Cnoc chaol

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The dead of the Great Wave counted

told_in.section: II. Of the Short Night

events.title: Ailean's tally-book of the wave begun
events.body: Ailean mac Iain, sent south with the relief party, opens a plain tally-book at Cuan dhearg and enters the first of what will be a summer's counting: boats found standing in the fields, wells fouled or sweet, dead named where they can be and marked only by place where they cannot.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The dead of the Great Wave counted

told_in.section: III. Of Cuan dhearg

events.title: The dead of Cuan dhearg buried on the rise
events.body: Through the first fortnight after the wave, the dead of Cuan dhearg are carried up onto the rise above the old harbour line and buried in ground the sea has not reached, while the town's clerks mark by place what names cannot be recovered.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The dead of the Great Wave counted

told_in.section: III. Of Cuan dhearg

events.title: The boats left standing in the barley
events.body: The wrecked fishing boats of Cuan dhearg, carried inland by the wave and left standing among the barley behind the town, are judged too many to right before winter and are left through the harvest, one still upright in its furrow with its mast stepped.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The dead of the Great Wave counted

told_in.section: III. Of Cuan dhearg

events.title: The treasury's first relief roll voted
events.body: On the count of a little over forty dead, the council votes seed and removal for the survivors of Achadh mhin out of the treasury without a due asked in return, over one councillor's question of cost, answered that a kingdom that finds silver for a roll of arms can find grain for its own dead.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Achadh mhin under salt

told_in.section: IV. Of the Count and the Relief

events.title: Ros gharbh's fleet counted on the headland
events.body: Ailean mac Iain walks the headland above Ros gharbh's harbour and counts the town's fishing fleet where the wave cast it, hull by hull, sound or stove, and carries the count south as proof that a town spared its people can still be ruined in its trade.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The dead of the Great Wave counted

told_in.section: IV. Of the Count and the Relief

events.title: A hill shire questions its new arms
events.body: A custodian's widow keeping a south-western shire's books asks the council's clerk whether a shire that never bore a badge under the old custody must bear one now, and is answered that any shire's writs are read faster at Cathair dhearg with a seal, borrowed beast or none, than without one.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The roll of arms

told_in.section: I. Of the Maoir and the Roll of Arms

events.title: Tòmas draws Clàr nan Suaicheantas
events.body: Tòmas, a mason's clerk before the war and a council clerk since, draws Clàr nan Suaicheantas for the maoir's seals, copying many of its charges from a book of arms left at Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir, so that lions and parrots and crocodiles come to stand on the seals of shires where none was ever seen.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The roll of arms

told_in.section: I. Of the Maoir and the Roll of Arms

events.title: Tonn
events.body: In the survivors' accounts gathered by the relief parties, 'tonn', wave, is used of anything sudden and overwhelming. Within a generation the sense is heard across the south: 'tha e san tonn', he is in the wave of it.

events.title: The wave's reach on Eilean mhin
events.body: The Great Wave passes also over the low island of Eilean mhin off the southern coast, where none then lived the year round. The shepherds who summered there do not go back.

events.title: Ros gharbh's boats rebuilt
events.body: Through the following year Ros gharbh borrows hulls from harbours the wave did not reach while shipwrights from beyond the gulf raise its fleet anew on the cleared beach, one keel at a time, until the last boat is launched and the town's people begin calling that whole year simply the bad year.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The dead of the Great Wave counted

told_in.section: V. Of the Word the Wave Left

events.title: Coinneach mac Ailein moves his court back under the market roof
events.body: When Baile Mòr mhòr's new courthouse is raised at last, Coinneach mac Ailein sits in it for a single sitting and moves his court back under the market roof among the fish-scales the week after; the two maoir after him do the same, and no one writes down why.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The maor of Baile Mòr mhòr

told_in.section: I. Of the Maoir and the Roll of Arms

events.title: The old human coinage withdrawn
events.body: All the humans' coin still in hand is cried down and ceases to be money. Within a year a new coinage of the Rìoghachd takes its place, minted with ink of coal dust in its seal.

events.title: The mint at Cathair dhearg
events.body: A mint is set up in the old human counting-house at Cathair dhearg under Fearchar mac Dhòmhnaill, called Fearchar Bonn. The seal of each coin is pressed with an ink ground from coal dust, so that a clipped coin shows the colour at its edge.

links.label: Caused by
links.title: The coal ink for the new dies

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Fearchar Bonn's four failed strikings

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Òrd Mhacha's blessing of the first striking

events.title: The northern savings voided
events.body: The Tuathaich households kept what savings they had in the humans' coin. Now it is withdrawn, and their savings are worth their weight in metal and no more. The Moot at Caol mhòr petitions the council for an exchange. The petition is received and filed.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Walter Hale's tally of the cried-down savings

links.label: Leads to
links.title: A maor's clerk carries the new coin north

links.label: Caused by
links.title: Tional nan Tuathach debates the wording of its petition

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The petition copied fair and sent twice

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Ailean mac Iain files Tional nan Tuathach's letter

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Hale sets down the answer he means to give Tional nan Tuathach

events.title: Walter Hale's tally of the cried-down savings
events.body: Walter Hale goes house to house at Caol mhòr with his day-book, counting what the town's households had kept back in the humans' coin now the council has cried it down. The sum comes to something over four hundred marks across better than two hundred households, none of it large, all of it now worth its weight as metal alone.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The northern savings voided

told_in.book: Of the Coin with the Coal in its Seal
told_in.section: I. Of the Boxes Under the Beds

events.title: Fearchar Bonn's four failed strikings
events.body: At the mint in the old counting-house at Cathair dhearg, Fearchar mac Dhòmhnaill spends a winter grinding coal dust fine enough to hold in a coin's seal without fouling the die, ruining four strikings of good silver before the ink and the binder are right. The fifth striking is shown to the treasury and kept.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The mint at Cathair dhearg

told_in.book: Of the Coin with the Coal in its Seal
told_in.section: II. Of the Mint at Cathair dhearg

events.title: Òrd Mhacha's blessing of the first striking
events.body: The first true coin of the Rìoghachd is blessed by Òrd Mhacha before it leaves the mint at Cathair dhearg, on the council's own instruction that the coal in its seal be reckoned a piece of the mountain carried out into every purse of the kingdom. The coin passes at the capital's markets within the month as though it had always been current.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The mint at Cathair dhearg

told_in.book: Of the Coin with the Coal in its Seal
told_in.section: II. Of the Mint at Cathair dhearg

events.title: A maor's clerk carries the new coin north
events.body: In the autumn a young clerk of a southern maor's office rides to Caol mhòr with the first struck coin Tional nan Tuathach has seen, and, asked how a household of the south is managing the exchange, answers that he does not rightly know, his own family's savings having gone on the rent before the crying-down.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The northern savings voided

told_in.book: Of the Coin with the Coal in its Seal
told_in.section: II. Of the Mint at Cathair dhearg

events.title: Tional nan Tuathach debates the wording of its petition
events.body: Tional nan Tuathach argues two evenings over a letter for the council, one voice wanting it to ask why the coin was cried down without warning north, another wanting no blame in it at all. Walter Hale's plain ask for a exchange mark for mark, without complaint, stands by the second evening nearly as he first wrote it.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The northern savings voided

told_in.book: Of the Coin with the Coal in its Seal
told_in.section: III. Of the Letter Received and Filed

events.title: Joseph Marlow's ploughshares
events.body: At Doire mhin in the north the smith Joseph Marlow melts down his neighbours' withdrawn coin and casts it into ploughshares, and sells them back at the cost of the charcoal. The Tuathaich songs name him yet.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Joseph Marlow's first ploughshare

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Marlow's charge fixed at the price of the charcoal

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Joseph Marlow's song first sung at Doire mhin

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Hale sets down the answer he means to give Tional nan Tuathach

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The first furrow cut with a coin-iron share

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Walter Hale walks to Doire mhin in the snow

events.title: The coin at Inis thais
events.body: At Inis thais on the south-west coast the new coin is scarce for most of the year, and the merchants trade in chits written on the paper of the house of the Stone. When the coin comes the chits are redeemed at the house's door, and the house keeps a tenth.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The house of Lia Fàil's chits redeemed at its door

events.title: Òrd Bhrìde given its doctrine
events.body: The Coal Rite, Òrd Bhrìde, the order that keeps Brìde's flame and Crom's stone, is given a settled doctrine within the Old Faith. Through the long ages it had kept its flame by custom and by no written creed; now its doctrine is built upon the leyline and the unbroken line of the coal-touched.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The unbroken line left open in doctrine

events.title: The first high custodian of the Rite
events.body: Dòmhnall mac Thormoid is named Àrd-choimheadaiche of Òrd Bhrìde and seated at Seann Skell on the southern coast, where the order's greatest house stands. His first charge is to write an order of worship. There had never been one.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The written order first read at the southern Seann Skell

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Copies of the order sent to every house of Deas-ghnàth a' Ghuail

events.title: The Hawk houses refuse
events.body: The houses of Òrd an t-Seabhaig about Cnoc bheag refuse the new order of worship, holding that the older form of the Old Faith needs no custodian above the local altar. They are not compelled. Here begins the long quarrel of the Hawk and the Rite.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Òrd an t-Seabhaig' letter of refusal

links.label: At the same time
links.title: Muileann naomh's bell first rung at a measured burning

events.title: The hawk-house at Muileann naomh takes the order
events.body: The hawk-house at Muileann naomh, southernmost of the Hawk's houses and farthest from Cnoc bheag, takes the Rite's written order of worship and becomes a house of Òrd Bhrìde. Its bell, the first hung in any hawk-house, now rings at the Rite's measured burnings. No other house of the Hawk follows.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Harry Marlow promised to a Cuan shean yard

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Dòmhnall mac Thormoid's book of correspondence begun

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Dòmhnall mac Thormoid thanks Muileann naomh

events.title: The petition copied fair and sent twice
events.body: David Hale copies his father's letter to the council a second time, so that one fair copy travels south with the winter carter and a second waits for the spring roads, on the reasoning that two letters in two hands are harder for a clerk to mislay than one. Both reach the council's chests within the year.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The northern savings voided

told_in.book: Of the Coin with the Coal in its Seal
told_in.section: III. Of the Letter Received and Filed

events.title: Ailean mac Iain files Tional nan Tuathach's letter
events.body: Tional nan Tuathach's letter asking an exchange for the north's voided savings reaches the council's chests and is read by the under-clerk Ailean mac Iain, who notes its date and seal, finds no standing order to answer it, and sets it down among that quarter's petitions marked with two words, received; filed, as his post requires.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The northern savings voided

told_in.book: Of the Coin with the Coal in its Seal
told_in.section: III. Of the Letter Received and Filed

events.title: Joseph Marlow's first ploughshare
events.body: At his forge by the millrace at Doire mhin, Joseph Marlow melts down his own household's cried-down coin before any neighbour's, casting it into the flat shape a ploughshare wants, still bearing along one edge the ghost of a king's profile the mould has not erased.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Joseph Marlow's ploughshares

told_in.book: Of the Coin with the Coal in its Seal
told_in.section: IV. Of Doire mhin in the Snow

events.title: Marlow's charge fixed at the price of the charcoal
events.body: Joseph Marlow sets his price for turning a neighbour's dead coin into a ploughshare at the cost of his charcoal alone, reasoning that a man should not pay twice for coin the council has already taken from him once. Half of Doire mhin brings him its savings before the winter is out.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Joseph Marlow's ploughshares

told_in.book: Of the Coin with the Coal in its Seal
told_in.section: IV. Of Doire mhin in the Snow

events.title: Harry Marlow promised to a Cuan shean yard
events.body: Harry Marlow, Joseph Marlow's eldest son, nine years old, is promised to a shipwright's yard at Cuan shean when he turns thirteen, on the word of a Cuan shean man who watched him true a plough-beam by eye at his father's forge without a level.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The hawk-house at Muileann naomh takes the order

told_in.book: Of the Coin with the Coal in its Seal
told_in.section: IV. Of Doire mhin in the Snow

events.title: Joseph Marlow's song first sung at Doire mhin
events.body: A plain tune naming Joseph Marlow and his forge is first heard going quietly round Doire mhin that winter, sung under the breath of the women waiting their turn with a sackful of savings, though the smith himself will not sing it in front of a stranger.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Joseph Marlow's ploughshares

told_in.book: Of the Coin with the Coal in its Seal
told_in.section: IV. Of Doire mhin in the Snow

events.title: The house of Lia Fàil's chits redeemed at its door
events.body: At Inis thais, where the new coin arrives slower than almost anywhere in the kingdom, the merchants trade the winter through on chits written against the word of the house of Òrd na Cloiche. When coin at last comes south in quantity, the chits are carried to the house's own door and redeemed there, less a tenth the house keeps for the keeping of them.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The coin at Inis thais

told_in.book: Of the Coin with the Coal in its Seal
told_in.section: V. Of the Chits at Inis thais, and the Turn

events.title: Hale sets down the answer he means to give Tional nan Tuathach
events.body: Weighing Fearchar Bonn's coin against Joseph Marlow's ploughshare on his own table, Walter Hale writes for Tional nan Tuathach that a people waiting on an answer that never comes would do better to build, while it waits, the thing it asked for, since the waiting will be long and the ground does not stop wanting to be ploughed.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The northern savings voided

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Joseph Marlow's ploughshares

told_in.book: Of the Coin with the Coal in its Seal
told_in.section: V. Of the Chits at Inis thais, and the Turn

events.title: The first furrow cut with a coin-iron share
events.body: At the end of am Màrt the first furrow of Doire mhin's spring ploughing is cut behind a borrowed ox with one of Joseph Marlow's shares, turning a clean black line the length of the field, the humans' silver made over into iron for a north the council's coin has not yet reached.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Joseph Marlow's ploughshares

told_in.book: Of the Coin with the Coal in its Seal
told_in.section: V. Of the Chits at Inis thais, and the Turn

events.title: Walter Hale walks to Doire mhin in the snow
events.body: Walter Hale walks the ten miles to Doire mhin in an Gearran on a road half snow and half black mud to see Joseph Marlow's forge for himself, and writes that the town had turned what the council left worthless into something a field could use without asking anyone's leave.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Joseph Marlow's ploughshares

told_in.book: Of the Coin with the Coal in its Seal
told_in.section: IV. Of Doire mhin in the Snow

events.title: The written order first read at the southern Seann Skell
events.body: In the hall of the greatest house of Deas-ghnàth a' Ghuail, Dòmhnall mac Thormoid reads aloud, for the first time, the order of worship he has spent the year composing: the leyline, the unbroken line of fuil-ghuail, and the measure of what may be burned. Eleven custodians and a scattering of witnesses from neighbouring houses hear it out in silence.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The first high custodian of the Rite

told_in.section: III. Of the First Reading

events.title: Òrd na Cloiche promise good will and nothing more
events.body: Within the month a letter reaches Seann Skell from Òrd na Cloiche in the south-west, wishing the new order well and offering no further part in it. Dòmhnall mac Thormoid copies it into the first page of a plain ledger he begins that day, meaning to keep every letter Deas-ghnàth a' Ghuail sends or receives from then on.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The houses of the Stone stand aside

told_in.section: III. Of the First Reading

events.title: Òrd an t-Seabhaig' letter of refusal
events.body: A letter comes to Seann Skell from Òrd an t-Seabhaig about Cnoc bheag, sealed with the mark of a bird with wings spread flat: the old form of Deas-ghnàth a' Ghuail has never needed a custodian above the local altar and sees no cause to answer to one now. It calls the new writing handsome, and not needed, and wishes the southern house no ill in going its own way.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The Hawk houses refuse

told_in.section: IV. Of the Cnoc bheag Letter and the Bell at Muileann naomh

events.title: Muileann naomh's bell first rung at a measured burning
events.body: The hawk-house at Muileann naomh, far south of Cnoc bheag, takes up the written order entire and hangs a bell cast new for the ordered worship, the first any house of Deas-ghnàth a' Ghuail has raised for that purpose rather than a wedding or a warning. It is rung that summer at the year's measured burning before a small crowd gathered in the lane.

links.label: At the same time
links.title: The Hawk houses refuse

told_in.section: IV. Of the Cnoc bheag Letter and the Bell at Muileann naomh

events.title: Dòmhnall mac Thormoid's book of correspondence begun
events.body: Watching a house answer him with silence rather than argument, the new Àrd-choimheadaiche begins a plain ledger to hold every letter Deas-ghnàth a' Ghuail sends or receives, the first such record any keeper of the flame has thought to make, so that a question once answered need not be answered from nothing a second time.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The hawk-house at Muileann naomh takes the order

told_in.section: I. Of the Letter that Found Him

events.title: Dòmhnall mac Thormoid rides north to Cathair dhearg
events.body: Summoned to be presented at court as Deas-ghnàth a' Ghuail's first Àrd-choimheadaiche, Dòmhnall mac Thormoid rides to the capital to press, unsuccessfully, for a share in Òrd Mhacha's keeping of the coronation regalia. He pays for his own lodging, no arrangement having been made for him, and returns south with only the high priest's refusal to enter in his book.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The crown's order and the court

told_in.section: V. Of the Regalia and the Refusal at Court

events.title: The unbroken line left open in doctrine
events.body: Writing the order's page on fuil-ghuail, Dòmhnall mac Thormoid finds an old defence and a later gloss disagree on whether the unbroken line means blood or office, and sets the doctrine down to hold both readings rather than close either, having found no ground in the record to choose between them.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Òrd Bhrìde given its doctrine

told_in.section: II. Of the Leyline and the Unbroken Line

events.title: Dòmhnall mac Thormoid thanks Muileann naomh
events.body: Dòmhnall mac Thormoid writes to the hawk-house at Muileann naomh in his own hand, the first letter of thanks he composes in his office, has it copied once for his ledger, and sends it back by the wool-trader who brought him word of the bell.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The hawk-house at Muileann naomh takes the order

told_in.section: IV. Of the Cnoc bheag Letter and the Bell at Muileann naomh

events.title: The houses of the Stone stand aside
events.body: The houses of Òrd na Cloiche in the south-west, whose Clach, the Lia Fàil, is not Crom's stone, are bidden to send witnesses to the settling of the Rite at Seann Skell. They send none, and a letter wishing it well.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Òrd na Cloiche promise good will and nothing more

events.title: The Moot's schoolhouse petition
events.body: Walter Hale asks the council for leave to open schools in the north that teach in the humans' tongue. The council answers that the kingdom's schools teach in Dia-thìris and it has no others. The Moot's minute calls the answer 'clear, at least'.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Tional nan Tuathach votes its school purse

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Walter Hale heard as a witness at Ceann mhòr

events.title: The crown's order and the court
events.body: The house of Òrd Mhacha at Cathair dhearg, the order of the capital and the crown, is given the keeping of the coronation regalia, which it had kept before the humans came. The Rite's high custodian asks a share in the keeping and is refused.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Dòmhnall mac Thormoid rides north to Cathair dhearg

events.title: The first census after the Severance
events.body: The state counts its own people for the first time since it took back the island. The roll notes, and says no more of it, how few the coal-touched are.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The census asks of faith and finds none to answer for some

events.title: The census of the faiths
events.body: The first census of the restored kingdom enters every town under the faith its people keep, the Old Faith, the Old Spirits or the Church. It is the first such roll since Seumas Bàn's clerks counted the rites at Dùn ìseal. On the far north-western cape beyond Baile chrom, where there is no town, the clerks find scattered families with no house of any faith, and on Eilean ghorm and the smallest islets no one to ask. All these they enter as *gun chreideamh*, without a faith.

events.title: The count taken from the road
events.body: Dia-thìrich census clerks count the Tuathaich towns of Siorrachd Doire ghlas from the road and enter few of the houses. That same year the Moot keeps its own tally. The two totals differ by nearly a fifth, and each side holds to its own.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The two counts of Doire ghlas go uncorrected

events.title: The circuit justices
events.body: Justices are appointed to ride circuit among the shires, and the first of them is Eilidh nic Leòid of Cathair dhomhain. Her circuit takes in eleven shires of the south-west and is most of a year in the riding.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Eilidh nic Leòid's letter of office reaches Cathair dhomhain

events.title: The head-due first collected
events.body: The maoir gather the head-due for the first time, on the households the census counted, at eighteen purses on every five thousand heads, and take it with the harbour dues.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Eilidh's first assize, held at Cathair dhomhain

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Eilidh's ruling on the Muileann bhàn well

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The head-due first gathered along the southern circuit

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Eilidh's circuit calls at Inis thais

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Eilidh's circuit calls at Doire shean

events.title: Copies of the order sent to every house of Deas-ghnàth a' Ghuail
events.body: By the last month of winter Dòmhnall mac Thormoid's two clerks finish fair copies of the order, each checked line by line against his own text, and he sends them to every house of An Creideamh Sean still standing, the Hawk-houses among them, along with Òrd na Cloiche, Òrd Mhacha, and a last copy carried back to Muileann naomh in thanks.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The first high custodian of the Rite

told_in.section: VII. Of the Copies Sent Out

events.title: The census asks of faith and finds none to answer for some
events.body: The state's first census, sent to ask what households hold to as well as how many they number, meets on the far north-western cape and its islets a good many who give no creed at all. Finding no word in Dia-thìris that fits a household with nothing to declare, the clerks write against their names gun chreideamh, without a creed, and ride on.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The first census after the Severance

told_in.section: I. Of the Two Counts of Doire ghlas

events.title: The two counts of Doire ghlas go uncorrected
events.body: The state's roll and Tional nan Tuathach's own tally of the northern shire, taken the same season by different hands, are found afterward to differ by close to a fifth. Neither is sent to the other side to be checked against it, and both are filed, each true by its own reckoning, in the chest that kept it.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The count taken from the road

told_in.section: I. Of the Two Counts of Doire ghlas

events.title: Eilidh nic Leòid's letter of office reaches Cathair dhomhain
events.body: A council rider, delayed three days by flooded roads, brings Eilidh nic Leòid the letter naming her first among Britheamhan na Cuairte: eleven shires of the south-west to be ridden once in every twelvemonth, and a written record of every judgment to be carried back each year to the council's clerks.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The circuit justices

told_in.section: II. Of Cathair dhomhain and the Custody-Book

events.title: Eilidh's first assize, held at Cathair dhomhain
events.body: Before setting out on her circuit Eilidh nic Leòid sits her first cases at home: a boundary measured with a knotted cord rather than taken on either party's word, a debt found on the strength of an unburned receipt, and a fishmonger's short weight proved against the council's own standard.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The head-due first collected

told_in.section: III. Of the First Assize and the Wells at Muileann bhàn

events.title: The quarrel over the well at Muileann bhàn
events.body: A widow who once charged a penny a season for water from a spring now run dry, and the mason set to warden the town's new waterworks, bring their dispute over one well to Britheamhan na Cuairte's bench in the mill-yard, the town having no courtroom of its own.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Muileann bhàn's waterworks

told_in.section: III. Of the First Assize and the Wells at Muileann bhàn

events.title: Eilidh's ruling on the Muileann bhàn well
events.body: The justice rules that the dead spring's old custom cannot be transferred to water drawn by a different road and paid for from a different purse, but that the well's ground remains the widow's by custom, and the town's word is given that it will never be built over or fenced from her without leave.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The head-due first collected

told_in.section: III. Of the First Assize and the Wells at Muileann bhàn

events.title: The head-due first gathered along the southern circuit
events.body: Maors' clerks set up their tables at the crossroads of the south-west shires and take the head-due, eighteen purses on every five thousand heads, for the first time in living memory. Eilidh nic Leòid, riding past more than one such table, keeps her own note of what she sees, though none of it is brought to her bench.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The head-due first collected

told_in.section: IV. Of the Head-Due and the Road South

events.title: Eilidh's circuit calls at Inis thais
events.body: The harbour court at Inis thais, kept well enough already by its own magistrate, hands up only two causes to the visiting justice, both turning on the ownership of a fishing boat after its owner died leaving no heir the town could agree on.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The head-due first collected

told_in.section: IV. Of the Head-Due and the Road South

events.title: Eilidh's circuit calls at Doire shean
events.body: Sitting two days in the temple porch for want of a courtroom, the justice settles a dispute among four households over the right to dry nets on a stretch of shingle by asking after the shore's own long custom rather than any written law, which none had ever thought to write so far down the coast.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The head-due first collected

told_in.section: IV. Of the Head-Due and the Road South

events.title: Muileann bhàn's waterworks
events.body: Muileann bhàn on the southern plain builds the first public waterworks of the restored kingdom: a stone tank on the hill, fed by the mill-race, with lead pipes to four street wells. The Guild of Hewers sends its surveyors to learn the making of it.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The quarrel over the well at Muileann bhàn

events.title: The Leòid ruling
events.body: Sitting at Seann Bhral, Eilidh nic Leòid rules that land held by Tuathaich under human title passes to the Crown, and that the right to work it stays with the holders and their heirs. The ruling is cited in nearly every land case of the age after.

links.label: Caused by
links.title: The margins of Breith Leòid

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The maor of Seann Bhral asks a ruling of his own cousin

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The Tanner suit heard at Seann Bhral in the west

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Breith Leòid copied to every maor's court of the circuit

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Murchadh Clàrc asks whether making law is strange

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The Dunlop title read to its end

events.title: The maor of Seann Bhral asks a ruling of his own cousin
