events.body: Artair mac Lachlainn, maor of the western shire, meets Britheamhan na Cuairte at the town gate and asks her plainly to find for An Crùn's grant, the household holding it being kin of his own. She hears the cause as she hears any other, and he sits through it without speaking.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The Leòid ruling

told_in.section: V. Of the Ruling at Seann Bhral

events.title: The Tanner suit heard at Seann Bhral in the west
events.body: A Tuathaich family holding four fields under a surveyor of A' Chompanaidh's title cut before An Dealachadh is set against a Dia-thìreach household holding An Crùn's newer grant of the same ground, made in ignorance that the land was occupied at all. Half the shire's Tuathaich households come to Seann Bhral to hear it argued.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The Leòid ruling

told_in.section: V. Of the Ruling at Seann Bhral

events.title: Breith Leòid copied to every maor's court of the circuit
events.body: Eilidh nic Leòid has her ruling fair-copied to every maor's court of her eleven shires, with a note that any like cause be decided on like reasoning until the council itself says otherwise, reasoning that a law read differently in every court that hears it is no law at all.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The Leòid ruling

told_in.section: VI. Of the Copy Sent to Every Court

events.title: Murchadh Clàrc asks whether making law is strange
events.body: On the road between Doire shean and Seann Bhral in the last days of an Lùnastal, Murchadh Clàrc asks Eilidh nic Leòid, not for the first time, whether she finds it strange to be making law rather than only keeping it, after so many years reading a book of rights settled before she was born.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The Leòid ruling

told_in.section: IV. Of the Head-Due and the Road South

events.title: The coal line repaired
events.body: The railway the humans built from the central mountains to the sea, broken in three places in the Severance war, is mended as far as Muileann chrom. A Rail Board is formed at Cathair dhearg to run it, with a clerk, two engineers and the humans' timetable.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Comhairle na Slighe-iarainn's timetable hung at Muileann chrom

events.title: The bridge at Cathair dhearg re-dedicated
events.body: The stone bridge over the Abhainn dhomhain below the capital, rebuilt in the humans' day, is hallowed anew with a name-stone in Dia-thìris. The humans' stone is left in its place and turned to face the river.

events.title: Comhairle na Slighe-iarainn's timetable hung at Muileann chrom
events.body: The mended line's copied timetable, carried over from the humans' own working papers, is hung on a board at the Muileann chrom terminus where the rails now end. Passengers and carters read it as they find it, since no one troubles to explain why a six-year-old kingdom keeps a dead people's hours.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The coal line repaired

told_in.book: Of the Vigil in the Open
told_in.section: I. Of the Line to Muileann chrom

events.title: The talk at the net-mending
events.body: Under the eaves of the net-store church at Baile chrom, the winter's net-mending turns to talk of Hannah Crane's word that Oidhche Glaise vigil will be kept in the open. Some call it needless risk to an old office; others say it is overdue. No one carries the talk beyond the town.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The Grey Night kept openly

told_in.book: Of the Vigil in the Open
told_in.section: III. Of the Night in the Open

events.title: The necropolis at Cnoc dhìreach
events.body: The shire of Ceann mhin closes the old burial ground at Tuam Cnoc dhìreach to new graves, for the vines have broken so many stones that no room can be found. Families of the town still tend the old graves, and some say the place is not empty after dark.

events.title: Eaglais nan Tuathach persists
events.body: The Tuathaich communities keep their Church alive in the north. Quietly they keep also the telling of the First Canoe, the voyage of Naomh Breandan to the Isle of the Blessed, which the Dia-thìrich priesthood calls superstition still.

events.title: The Grey Night kept openly
events.body: At Baile chrom in the far north-west the vigil-keeper Hannah Crane holds the vigil of Rùn-dìomhair na h-Oidhche Glaise in the open, for the first time since the Severance. The sect keeps one night of silence in the year under Sìne, the Peaceful Goose, its name for the wild goose of the Holy Spirit. The bishops of the Church call the vigil irregular. Outsiders are not told which night it is.

links.label: Caused by
links.title: The talk at the net-mending

links.label: Caused by
links.title: The old priest's counsel

links.label: At the same time
links.title: The maor's man watches and writes nothing

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The bishops' letter kept behind the altar-cloth

links.label: At the same time
links.title: A young wife of Muileann fhionn keeps her own watch

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Oidhche Glaise kept in the open a second year

events.title: The churches of the north
events.body: Most Tuathaich towns keep An Eaglais, the Church their forebears brought at the Crossing; the Dia-thìrich of the west coast beside them keep Manannan's order. A church is built at Cnoc ghorm, the greatest in the north.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The Ros bheag bell raised at Cnoc ghorm

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The Cnoc ghorm bell heard on the shore road

events.title: The cattle-market at Muileann fhionn
events.body: Muileann fhionn, the mill-town the humans built to guard the northern landing, is granted a market right for the north-western inland country. The Tuathaich drovers bring their cattle and sheep to it, and from it the droves go south to Ceann leathan and the farms of the south-east. It grows to be the greatest cattle-market on the island.

links.label: Caused by
links.title: The hurdles built on the Muileann fhionn green

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The first drove south from Muileann fhionn

events.title: The old priest's counsel
events.body: Walking back from a burial, the priest of Baile chrom tells Hannah Crane that the vigil's keeping is hers to judge, having held his own office forty years by staying out of what belongs to another. It is the only word of encouragement she has from anyone before the night.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The Grey Night kept openly

told_in.book: Of the Vigil in the Open
told_in.section: III. Of the Night in the Open

events.title: The maor's man watches and writes nothing
events.body: A clerk's assistant of Cnoc ghorm, lodging at Baile chrom on an unrelated errand, climbs a rise above the headland and watches Hannah Crane's vigil through the night from a distance. He carries no instruction to report it and no form to record it on, and the shire's returns for the week say nothing.

links.label: At the same time
links.title: The Grey Night kept openly

told_in.book: Of the Vigil in the Open
told_in.section: III. Of the Night in the Open

events.title: The bishops' letter kept behind the altar-cloth
events.body: Three bishops of An Eaglais write to Baile chrom calling the open keeping of Oidhche Glaise irregular, and ask, without commanding, that the custom be given up. Hannah Crane reads the letter twice and puts it away in the box that already keeps the town's oldest relic, and answers nothing.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The Grey Night kept openly

told_in.book: Of the Vigil in the Open
told_in.section: IV. Of the Letter Called Irregular

events.title: The Ros bheag bell raised at Cnoc ghorm
events.body: The bell of the old chapel at Ros bheag, carted north at An Dealachadh and crated in a barn for want of a tower to take it, is hung at last in the new church at Cnoc ghorm and rung on a market morning. Its sound carries to the shore road, farther than the town had thought a single bell could reach.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The churches of the north

told_in.book: Of the Vigil in the Open
told_in.section: IV. Of the Letter Called Irregular

events.title: The hurdles built on the Muileann fhionn green
events.body: The town's carpenters spend most of a month raising pens on the old common green at Muileann fhionn, working from a plan one of them had seen used at a southern fair, to hold the cattle and sheep the new market right will bring down from the hill farms.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The cattle-market at Muileann fhionn

told_in.book: Of the Vigil in the Open
told_in.section: V. Of the Geese Going North

events.title: The first drove south from Muileann fhionn
events.body: Hill farmers who had always walked their beasts the long way south now bring them to the new market at Muileann fhionn, and from there the droves go on by the old tracks toward Ceann leathan. Within a few seasons the green stands trodden to mud on every market morning.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The cattle-market at Muileann fhionn

told_in.book: Of the Vigil in the Open
told_in.section: V. Of the Geese Going North

events.title: A young wife of Muileann fhionn keeps her own watch
events.body: A woman newly married into Baile chrom from Muileann fhionn, who asked Hannah Crane whether she was not afraid to keep the vigil alone, climbs the headland herself the night it is kept and watches from a careful distance. She tells no one, not even her husband, that she went.

links.label: At the same time
links.title: The Grey Night kept openly

told_in.book: Of the Vigil in the Open
told_in.section: III. Of the Night in the Open

events.title: The Cnoc ghorm bell heard on the shore road
events.body: On the new church's first market morning the Ros bheag bell in Cnoc ghorm's tower carries out past the fields to the shore road, and carters driving in from Muileann fhionn hear it and know, before they see the tower, that Cnoc ghorm has a church worth the name.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The churches of the north

told_in.book: Of the Vigil in the Open
told_in.section: IV. Of the Letter Called Irregular

events.title: The church school at Cnoc ghorm
events.body: The church at Cnoc ghorm opens a school for its priests. It teaches in the humans' tongue and reads the Bible in the Dia-thìris text its preachers use on the west coast. In all the north, both are taught there only.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The Cnoc ghorm church school opens its first term

events.title: The border wall proposed
events.body: A fixed boundary between the Dia-thìrich and the Tuathaich country is proposed for the first time. It is refused as needless, for the two peoples already keep apart of their own will.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Seumas mac Coinnich Ghlais proposes a marked boundary

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The council lets the wall stand unbuilt

events.title: The minute on the wall
events.body: The council minute that refuses the boundary wall runs to four lines. The fourth reads: 'They do not come south.' Five of the twelve councillors initial it; the other seven do not sign against it.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The minute on the wall signed by five, opposed by none

events.title: The Allt an Àigh walk
events.body: The followers of Na Seann Spioradan keep their yearly walk to the holy well called Allt an Àigh in the east, whose water, the old tales say, brings fortune. The custodians of the Rite speak against the walk and do not forbid it.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Gormshuil begins a book of her own

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Gormshuil walks to Allt an Àigh with her mother

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Gormshuil parts from her mother at Ceann àrsaidh

events.title: Oidhche Glaise kept in the open a second year
events.body: Oidhche Glaise is kept in the open on the headland below the light at Baile chrom the year after the bishops' letter and the year after that, on nights Hannah Crane tells no one in advance; no bishop comes north to see for himself what irregular meant.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The Grey Night kept openly

told_in.book: Of the Vigil in the Open
told_in.section: IV. Of the Letter Called Irregular

events.title: The Cnoc ghorm church school opens its first term
events.body: Nine boys sit the first term of the school raised inside the new church at Cnoc ghorm, taught the humans' tongue and the western reading of the scripture by a master brought up from Seann Skell. The letter reporting it to the council asks for nothing and is filed without debate.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The church school at Cnoc ghorm

told_in.book: Of the Wall that was Not Built
told_in.section: I. Of the School Reported

events.title: Seumas mac Coinnich Ghlais proposes a marked boundary
events.body: The councillor of the eastern custodian houses lays a map before the council and asks for a ditch and bank, with stones set at the mile, along the line where the settled shires meet the Tuathaich country, arguing that a boundary kept only in memory will not hold as both peoples' numbers grow.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The border wall proposed

told_in.book: Of the Wall that was Not Built
told_in.section: II. Of the Wall Proposed

events.title: The council lets the wall stand unbuilt
events.body: After two hours' debate on cost and custom, an old councillor says plainly that in eight years no Tuathaich has crossed where he was not wanted, and the room presses the boundary no further. No vote is taken; the proposal is simply not renewed by anyone present.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The border wall proposed

told_in.book: Of the Wall that was Not Built
told_in.section: II. Of the Wall Proposed

events.title: The minute on the wall signed by five, opposed by none
events.body: Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill's four-line minute, ending in the sentence spoken against the wall, is initialled by five of the twelve councillors. The other seven enter no dissent. An Leabharlann keeps the sheet as the whole of the boundary's history: proposed, weighed, and left undrawn.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The minute on the wall

told_in.book: Of the Wall that was Not Built
told_in.section: II. Of the Wall Proposed

events.title: Gormshuil begins a book of her own
events.body: Keeping the blotted first draft of the wall's minute rather than burning it, the under-clerk pastes it into a small board-bound book bought without her clerk-master's knowledge and begins, that same evening, a private record of her own, the first of the volumes she keeps for the rest of her working life.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The Allt an Àigh walk

told_in.book: Of the Wall that was Not Built
told_in.section: II. Of the Wall Proposed

events.title: Gormshuil walks to Allt an Àigh with her mother
events.body: Given a fortnight's leave for the first time in two years, the under-clerk walks the old road east with her mother, of an Old Spirits house, to drink at the holy well and add a stone to its cairn, lodging a night on the way at the walkers' hall of Achadh gharbh.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The Allt an Àigh walk

told_in.book: Of the Wall that was Not Built
told_in.section: III. Of the Walk to Allt an Àigh

events.title: The walkers' ledger at Achadh gharbh
events.body: The keeper of the hall built for the well's pilgrims shows Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill her cracked-spined ledger of every walker's shire and name, its pages already holding travellers from better than twenty shires, north and south and east and west of the island together on the one road.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The walkers at Achadh gharbh

told_in.book: Of the Wall that was Not Built
told_in.section: III. Of the Walk to Allt an Àigh

events.title: The mountain's yield passes the humans' own figure
events.body: A surveyor's report tells the council, in the flat language such reports keep, that the mine's yield has come back to what it gave under the humans and, in the month just past, gone beyond it, the working unchanged in every particular but the hands the profit now fills.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The mine worked to the full again

told_in.book: Of the Wall that was Not Built
told_in.section: IV. Of the Sloc Mòr

events.title: Gormshuil parts from her mother at Ceann àrsaidh
events.body: Walking home from Allt an Àigh, Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill and her mother part on the eastern road at Ceann àrsaidh, her mother turning north to her own village and Gormshuil south to the capital; her mother says only that she is glad the walk was given her that year, and asks nothing of the council's business.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The Allt an Àigh walk

told_in.book: Of the Wall that was Not Built
told_in.section: III. Of the Walk to Allt an Àigh

events.title: The walkers at Achadh gharbh
events.body: The walkers to Allt an Àigh lodge at Achadh gharbh on the way, and the village builds a long hall for them. The hall's keeper writes each walker's shire in a book, and by the end of the decade it holds names from fifty shires.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The walkers' ledger at Achadh gharbh

events.title: The mine worked to the full again
events.body: The mine's yield after the Severance comes up to what it gave under the humans, and then passes it. The working is the same as before. Only the profit goes to other hands.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The mountain's yield passes the humans' own figure

events.title: The Sloc Mòr concession
events.body: The Crown grants the working of the Sloc Mòr, the great shaft at Achadh dhomhain, to Uisdean mac Ùisdein of Cathair mhòr, whose house held an overseer's post under the humans. The Crown takes a fifth of the yield. The terms are the humans' terms with the names changed.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: An Sloc Mòr granted to Uisdean mac Ùisdein

events.title: The night-shift kept
events.body: The council will not end the working of the vein by day and night that the humans ordered two generations before. The mountain is still given no season of rest. The custodians of the Rite enter a protest, and then bless the shafts.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: A board is seated over An Sloc Mòr's grant

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Uisdean mac Ùisdein's first contract with the hewers

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The council lets the night shift stand

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The custodians enter their protest against the unresting shaft

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Gormshuil reads the grant at the shaft-head

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The custodians bless the shafts they could not close

events.title: An Sloc Mòr granted to Uisdean mac Ùisdein
events.body: Uisdean mac Ùisdein of Cathair mhòr, whose family held an overseer's post there under the humans, comes to the capital to put his name to the working of the great shaft at Achadh dhomhain, the terms copied almost word for word from the humans' own ledgers save the fifth now kept for An Crùn.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The Sloc Mòr concession

told_in.book: Of the Wall that was Not Built
told_in.section: IV. Of the Sloc Mòr

events.title: A board is seated over An Sloc Mòr's grant
events.body: Three clerks and an engineer are set at a table in the council's own house at Cathair dhearg to see the mine's grant kept to its terms, answering to no name grander than the mountain itself, and it is to this small board, not the council, that Uisdean mac Ùisdein afterward sends his returns.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The night-shift kept

told_in.book: Of the Wall that was Not Built
told_in.section: IV. Of the Sloc Mòr

events.title: Uisdean mac Ùisdein's first contract with the hewers
events.body: Before the snow closes the high tracks, Uisdean mac Ùisdein rides north to set his name against the hewers' own at the shaft-head, the roster and the rates of pay carried over unaltered from the rolls the humans had kept, only the name at the head of the page now his own.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The night-shift kept

told_in.book: Of the Wall that was Not Built
told_in.section: IV. Of the Sloc Mòr

events.title: The council lets the night shift stand
events.body: Asked whether the mountain, now the island's own, should be given the rest the humans never allowed it, the mine board's engineer answers that the very yield just reported depends on a shaft that never stands idle, and the council sets the question aside rather than decide it either way.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The night-shift kept

told_in.book: Of the Wall that was Not Built
told_in.section: V. Of the Night Shift and the Blessing

events.title: The custodians enter their protest against the unresting shaft
events.body: The custodian houses of the vein carry down a half-page paper asking not that the night shift end, which they know is no longer the council's to give back, but only that their protest stand written, so that none after can say the old custom's breaking went unmarked.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The night-shift kept

told_in.book: Of the Wall that was Not Built
told_in.section: V. Of the Night Shift and the Blessing

events.title: Gormshuil reads the grant at the shaft-head
events.body: Sent north with the council's own copy of An Sloc Mòr grant, Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill reads it aloud to the assembled hewers by lamplight in the winter cold, the custodians of the shaft standing apart in their grey coats while the words that answer their protest with silence are read over their heads.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The night-shift kept

told_in.book: Of the Wall that was Not Built
told_in.section: V. Of the Night Shift and the Blessing

events.title: The custodians bless the shafts they could not close
events.body: Once the grant is read, the four custodians of the vein walk to the pit-mouth and speak an old blessing over it, calling on the mountain to hold, to give, and in its own time to rest, before turning back without further word to the lamps that burn on through the falling dark.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The night-shift kept

told_in.book: Of the Wall that was Not Built
told_in.section: V. Of the Night Shift and the Blessing

events.title: The pit towns fill
events.body: Dia-thìrich families from the hungry east go to the vein-towns for wages. Muileann dhearg doubles in size within three years. Its hall of the druid school, shut since the humans' time, is taken for a hewers' lodging and twice enlarged in those same years.

links.label: Same place
links.title: Iain mac Ruairidh taken on as chainman

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The druid hall at Muileann dhearg becomes a lodging

links.label: Leads to
links.title: A woman from Baile ruadh asks after walls

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Lachlann mac Iain Bhàin's book of the faces

events.title: Baile thais grows on the coal road
events.body: At Baile thais the coal road from the central mountains comes down to the Abhainn uaine above the gulf, and the town takes in carters, inns and a ropewalk. Its people double in a decade, and it is given a shire court.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Inns and a ropewalk at Baile thais

events.title: Raiders off Cathair gheal
events.body: Ships that fly no flag, some manned by men who once served the human administration, begin to raid the coast off Cathair gheal in the north-west. The Tuathaich towns suffer first, and no one defends them.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The raiders' first season off Cathair gheal

events.title: The coal line reaches the Sloc Mòr
events.body: The mended railway is carried up the valley to the pithead at Achadh dhomhain. The first coal train runs from the Sloc Mòr to Cathair dhearg in the kingdom's name, on the humans' rails.

links.label: Same place
links.title: The first coal train runs to the capital

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Colin Rudd drives the first coal train

events.title: Iain mac Ruairidh taken on as chainman
events.body: Iain, a hewer's son of the hills, is taken on by Lachlann mac Iain Bhàin, Comhairle nam Mèinnean's surveyor, to carry the chain and keep the faces' book at An Sloc Mòr. He is sworn to no guild, only entered on Comhairle nam Mèinnean's roll.

links.label: Same place
links.title: The pit towns fill

told_in.section: I. Of the Lamp and the Chain

events.title: The druid hall at Muileann dhearg becomes a lodging
events.body: As hungry families from the east crowd into the vein-towns, Muileann dhearg's shut druid hall is opened again, not for its old teaching but for pallets on its floor, and is twice enlarged within a few years to hold them.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The pit towns fill

told_in.section: II. Of the Towns that Filled

events.title: Inns and a ropewalk at Baile thais
events.body: The crossing at Baile thais, where Rathad na Mèinne meets the Abhainn uaine, fills with carters who stay the night and then keep families there; inns, stables and a ropewalk making the cages' hauling-rope grow up along the ford within the decade.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Baile thais grows on the coal road

told_in.section: II. Of the Towns that Filled

events.title: The raiders' first season off Cathair gheal
events.body: Flagless ships work the water off Cathair gheal in the north-west; a fishing house is burned on the shore below Cathair gheal and two boats are lost from Cathair gheal's own harbour. The council's word, when it comes the next spring, is four lines asking that the matter be watched.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Raiders off Cathair gheal

told_in.section: II. Of the Towns that Filled

events.title: The first coal train runs to the capital
events.body: On the third of an Dàmhair the mended rail carries the first train, loaded with coal cut that week, from An Sloc Mòr's pithead at Achadh dhomhain down to Cathair dhearg on the humans' own iron, a Tuathaich engineer at the footplate.

links.label: Same place
links.title: The coal line reaches the Sloc Mòr

told_in.section: III. Of the First Train

events.title: The Mac Ùisdein quarry-mark first cut
events.body: The grey, black-veined spoil of An Sloc Mòr's deeper galleries is quarried and dressed for building, and sold south under a stylised wave, the mark of Taigh Mhic Ùisdein, cut into every squared block.

links.label: Same place
links.title: The quarry at Achadh dhomhain

told_in.section: III. Of the First Train

events.title: Colin Rudd drives the first coal train
events.body: The engine of the first coal train from An Sloc Mòr to Cathair dhearg is driven by a Tuathaich man, Colin Rudd, who had oiled locomotives under the humans' foremen as a boy, and who takes it as no insult that the old custodian says his blessing over the coal in the first wagon rather than over the engine.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The coal line reaches the Sloc Mòr

told_in.section: III. Of the First Train

events.title: A woman from Baile ruadh asks after walls
events.body: A woman newly down from Baile ruadh with three children asks Iain mac Ruairidh, marking the Muileann dhearg lodging for Comhairle nam Mèinnean, whether Comhairle nam Mèinnean means to build proper walls or only to go on stacking families under one roof; he has no answer but that he surveys the ground and does not build on it.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The pit towns fill

told_in.section: II. Of the Towns that Filled

events.title: The quarry at Achadh dhomhain
events.body: The spoil of the Sloc Mòr, a grey stone veined with black, is cut and sold for building under the quarry-mark of the house of Mac Ùisdein. For forty years after it is used in public buildings across the south.

links.label: Same place
links.title: The Mac Ùisdein quarry-mark first cut

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Comhairle na Slighe-iarainn's office raised at Cathair dhearg

events.title: The shunting yards at Muileann chrom
events.body: The Rail Board lays new sidings at Muileann chrom, where the coal trains from the Sloc Mòr are broken up and made up again for the ports. The families of the yard, who work the small engines that move the wagons, are counted apart by the Board and live apart in rows beside the lines.

links.label: Same place
links.title: The first dubhan tank at Muileann chrom

links.label: Same place
links.title: A boy of the yard rows killed

links.label: Same place
links.title: The shunting yard at Muileann chrom counted apart

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The spur to Àth leathan opened

links.label: Leads to
links.title: A shunting driver asked his name

events.title: The western branch
events.body: The Rail Board carries a branch of the coal line west from Cathair dhearg to the port of Seann Bhral, with a spur north to the pits at Àth leathan, so that the western workings may send their coal east by rail.

events.title: The guilds restored
events.body: The old custom of binding apprentices, from the Holy Age, is taken up again in a changed form. It is now kept for Dia-thìrich alone.

events.title: The Guild of Hewers chartered
events.body: The first guild under the restored custom, the Guild of Hewers, is chartered at Achadh dhomhain. Its oath is sworn with a hand on a piece of coal. By the charter its rolls are open to Dia-thìrich only.

links.label: Same place
links.title: Comann nan Gualadairean chartered at Achadh dhomhain

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Iain mac Ruairidh stands outside the oath

events.title: Comhairle na Slighe-iarainn's office raised at Cathair dhearg
events.body: Comhairle na Slighe-iarainn builds its office at Cathair dhearg, low and of the same grey Mac Ùisdein stone, and Comhairle na Slighe-iarainn's business, surveys among them, is thereafter kept within its walls.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The quarry at Achadh dhomhain

told_in.section: IV. Of the Sidings and the Spur

events.title: Lachlann mac Iain Bhàin's book of the faces
events.body: Lachlann mac Iain Bhàin, Comhairle nam Mèinnean's surveyor at An Sloc Mòr, keeps a running book of the faces he and his chainman measure, entering each true figure against the hewers who are paid by the fathom driven.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The pit towns fill

told_in.section: I. Of the Lamp and the Chain

events.title: The shunting yard at Muileann chrom counted apart
events.body: New sidings at Muileann chrom, where An Sloc Mòr's coal trains are broken up and made up for the ports, bring rows of housing for the families who work the small engines. Comhairle na Slighe-iarainn keeps their roll separate from the shire's and houses them apart, beside the lines.

links.label: Same place
links.title: The shunting yards at Muileann chrom

told_in.section: IV. Of the Sidings and the Spur

events.title: The spur to Àth leathan opened
events.body: Comhairle na Slighe-iarainn lays thirteen miles of new rail off the western branch to Àth leathan, where Tuathaich hewers have long worked the coal, judging the ground poor but the coal cheap to lift and the carters' road worse each winter.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The shunting yards at Muileann chrom

told_in.section: IV. Of the Sidings and the Spur

events.title: Comann nan Gualadairean chartered at Achadh dhomhain
events.body: The restored custom of binding, kept now for Dia-thìrich alone, is set into Comann nan Gualadairean' charter and read aloud at Achadh dhomhain. Each hewer taken in lays a hand flat on a lump of coal and swears to keep the guild's custom, take no outside work and teach no craft of it to a hand unsworn.

links.label: Same place
links.title: The Guild of Hewers chartered

told_in.section: V. Of the Oath on the Coal

events.title: Iain mac Ruairidh stands outside the oath
events.body: At the guild's chartering Iain watches his own father sworn among the hewers and understands that the charter's rolls, open to those who cut, haul or timber the coal, hold no place for Comhairle nam Mèinnean's chainman who only measures where it lies.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The Guild of Hewers chartered

told_in.section: V. Of the Oath on the Coal

events.title: A shunting driver asked his name
events.body: Waiting an hour for the onward train at Muileann chrom, Iain mac Ruairidh walks out along the shunting rows and falls into talk with a driver named Murchadh, who has worked the humans' small engines since he was twelve and has never in thirty years been asked his name by anyone from the south.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The shunting yards at Muileann chrom

told_in.section: IV. Of the Sidings and the Spur

events.title: The shipwrights of Ros dhomhain
events.body: The shipwrights of Ros dhomhain take a guild charter of their own and bind their first thirty apprentices in a single day on the slipway.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: A Tuathaich boy's plea refused at the Ros dhomhain guild court

events.title: The indentures broken
events.body: At Cuan shean and Seann Bhral the Tuathaich boys already bound to Dia-thìrich masters are loosed from their indentures under the charter rule. Some go north. Most stay on as day-labourers, outside the guilds and their wages.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Harry Marlow's indenture torn at Cuan shean

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The Tuathaich day-wage set at the Cuan shean yard

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Tional nan Tuathach's letter on the indentures filed

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The torn indenture kept on the bench

events.title: The chandlers of Ceann àrsaidh
events.body: The ship-chandlers of Ceann àrsaidh, on the Abhainn fhionn east of the capital, take a guild charter and the sole right to supply the Crown's patrol boats. The right outlasts the boats.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The chandlers' patrol-boat right first exercised

events.title: The lamp-makers of Muileann mhin
events.body: The lamp-makers of Muileann mhin, who make the coal lamps of every shaft on the island, are chartered as a guild. Their mark, a flame over a hammer, is stamped on every lamp. Of all the guild marks, the humans' traders copied this one only.

links.label: Caused by
links.title: The first dubhan pit-lamps of Muileann mhin

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The lamp-makers' mark first stamped

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Harry Marlow measures the old wreck at Cuan shean

links.label: Leads to
links.title: A northern passage offered and refused at Cuan shean

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Harry Marlow sends his wage north at half rate

events.title: Harry Marlow's indenture torn at Cuan shean
events.body: Seumas Crùbach, shipwright of Cuan shean, takes down and tears the four-year indenture binding Harry Marlow to his yard, the guild court's charter rule having reached the coast that spring. He keeps Harry on the bench as a free hand rather than take a new bound apprentice in his place.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The indentures broken

told_in.section: IV. Of the Day-Labour

events.title: The Tuathaich day-wage set at the Cuan shean yard
events.body: Seumas Crùbach keeps Harry Marlow at half a bound man's wage and no guild standing once the indenture is loosed, a rate other yards along the coast take up that spring for the Tuathaich hands they keep on without a guild's leave to teach them.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The indentures broken

told_in.section: III. Of the Eight-and-Twentieth of am Màrt

events.title: A Tuathaich boy's plea refused at the Ros dhomhain guild court
events.body: A rope-maker's apprentice of four years' standing at Ros dhomhain brings his case to the newly chartered guild court and is heard and refused in a single sitting, the court ruling that the charter's custom of binding names Dia-thìrich hands alone.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The shipwrights of Ros dhomhain

told_in.section: II. Of the News from Ros dhomhain

events.title: Tional nan Tuathach's letter on the indentures filed
events.body: Tional nan Tuathach writes to the guild court at Cathair dhearg asking what is to become of the Tuathaich indentures already standing when the guilds' charters are read. The letter is filed among that year's business without an answer.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The indentures broken

told_in.section: II. Of the News from Ros dhomhain

events.title: The lamp-makers' mark first stamped
events.body: The lamp-makers of Muileann mhin, chartered that winter, set their mark, a flame struck over a hammer, on every coal lamp leaving their sheds from that year on, so that the lamp itself carries the record of where it was made and under what oath.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The lamp-makers of Muileann mhin

told_in.section: II. Of the News from Ros dhomhain

events.title: The chandlers' patrol-boat right first exercised
events.body: The newly chartered chandlers of Ceann àrsaidh fit out An Crùn's patrol boats under their sole right that spring, and the fitting-out becomes the guild's yearly show of its charter before the shire's maor.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The chandlers of Ceann àrsaidh

told_in.section: II. Of the News from Ros dhomhain

events.title: Harry Marlow measures the old wreck at Cuan shean
events.body: Freed from bound hours by the loosing of his indenture, Harry Marlow spends the year's stolen hours setting down in his own book the full lines of a derelict human hull left on the Cuan shean hard, learning by his own measure how a hull built plank first and framed after is made to hold together.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The lamp-makers of Muileann mhin

told_in.section: IV. Of the Day-Labour

events.title: A northern passage offered and refused at Cuan shean
events.body: A cloth trader out of Seann Vell, putting in at Cuan shean that autumn, tells Harry Marlow a free hand might do better in a northern harbour, where no guild court stands over a craftsman's work. Harry thanks him and stays at his bench.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The lamp-makers of Muileann mhin

told_in.section: IV. Of the Day-Labour

events.title: Harry Marlow sends his wage north at half rate
events.body: At the year's end Harry Marlow sends north to his father Joseph Marlow's forge at Doire mhin the sum he has set aside from a free hand's half-wage, a smaller sum than any year of his bound apprenticeship, kept from the same habit regardless.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The lamp-makers of Muileann mhin

told_in.section: IV. Of the Day-Labour

events.title: The torn indenture kept on the bench
events.body: Seumas Crùbach keeps the two torn halves of Harry Marlow's indenture on his bench through the whole year, moving them from shelf to shelf but never putting them to the fire, and when a stranger asks how his boy does, answers as he always had.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The indentures broken

told_in.section: IV. Of the Day-Labour

events.title: The weavers of Baile chiar
events.body: The weavers of Baile chiar are chartered as a guild. Their cloth of southern wool undersells the northern cloth at the fair, until the mills of Doire ghlas are built.

links.label: Same place
links.title: Baile chiar's weavers take a guild charter

events.title: Agnes Pike's school
events.body: Agnes Pike, a Tuathaich teacher, opens a school at Doire ghlas that teaches in the humans' tongue, with the Moot's money and without the council's leave. Within ten years there are nine such schools in the north. The council never licenses them and never shuts them.

links.label: Caused by
links.title: Ellen Marsh offers her schoolroom

links.label: Caused by
links.title: The bindery in Agnes Pike's school

links.label: Caused by
links.title: Tional nan Tuathach votes its school purse

links.label: Caused by
links.title: Walter Hale carries the school purse north

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Agnes Pike's school opens on the fourteenth of am Faoilleach

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Daniel Frayne walks in from Muileann leathan

links.label: At the same time
links.title: The maor visits the byre school and writes nothing

links.label: At the same time
links.title: Alice Hale opens a second school at Caol mhòr

events.title: The Cill ghlas district reopened
events.body: The mining district shut since the Rending is surveyed and declared safe to work. On the surveyors' word the first new shafts are cut well back from the old fault line.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The Cill ghlas fault line walked and found unmoved

events.title: The Leòid circuit in the north
events.body: Eilidh nic Leòid rides the northern circuit for the first time and holds court at Ceann mhòr. Of the nineteen cases brought before her, seventeen are Tuathaich suits over land. In fifteen she finds for the Crown, citing her own ruling.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: A widow lends her byre at Doire ghlas

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The school's register begun

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Daniel Frayne's fair copies pinned to the byre wall

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The school moves to the church porch for summer

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Daniel Frayne copies the minute of the school's own founding

links.label: Same place
links.title: Eilidh nic Leòid opens the Ceann mhòr assize

links.label: Same place
links.title: The Dunlop title read to its end

links.label: Same place
links.title: Fifteen suits found for An Crùn at Ceann mhòr

links.label: Same place
links.title: A custodian's countersign found on the Coombe title

links.label: Same place
links.title: The Coombes and the Pettifers found for the holders

links.label: Same place
links.title: Walter Hale heard as a witness at Ceann mhòr

links.label: Same place
links.title: Tional nan Tuathach's minute-books credited by a Crown bench

links.label: Same place
links.title: Hale and Eilidh nic Leòid speak at the Ceann mhòr inn

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Eilidh nic Leòid at the Seann Bhral harbour wall

events.title: Baile chiar's weavers take a guild charter
events.body: The council's clerks cut a new seal, a shuttle over a fleece, for the weavers of Baile chiar, entering the grant in a book bound in calf at Cathair dhearg after a fee is paid and a feast given. It is a charter of the ordinary kind: coin changes hands, a form is followed, and a craft already practised becomes a craft the kingdom has agreed to notice.

links.label: Same place
links.title: The weavers of Baile chiar

told_in.section: I. Of the Weavers and the Byre

events.title: Tional nan Tuathach votes its school purse
events.body: Tional nan Tuathach sets aside money of its own for a schoolroom at Doire ghlas, without asking the council's leave a second time, Walter Hale having judged that a council which says no once will say no as often as it is asked.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The Moot's schoolhouse petition

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Agnes Pike's school

told_in.section: II. Of the Fourteenth of am Faoilleach

events.title: A widow lends her byre at Doire ghlas
events.body: Jenny Marrow, whose husband's cattle a fever and a wet spring had thinned to a few head, offers her byre for the winter months in exchange for nothing but a promise that she and the children will be taught to write their names.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The Leòid circuit in the north

told_in.section: I. Of the Weavers and the Byre

events.title: Walter Hale carries the school purse north
events.body: Walter Hale rides the coast road himself to bring Agnes Pike Tional nan Tuathach's money the evening before her school opens, and leaves with it a sheet in his own hand setting out that the purse is Tional nan Tuathach's, the room the widow's, and the leave nobody's at all.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Agnes Pike's school

told_in.section: II. Of the Fourteenth of am Faoilleach

events.title: Agnes Pike's school opens on the fourteenth of am Faoilleach
events.body: Eleven children come through the byre door at Doire ghlas before An Eaglais bell finishes its stroke, to be taught their letters from am Bìoball and from a lent volume of Tional nan Tuathach's own minutes, there being no primer printed for the humans' tongue on the island.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Agnes Pike's school

told_in.section: II. Of the Fourteenth of am Faoilleach

events.title: The school's register begun
events.body: Agnes Pike opens a register for the byre school in its first week, its first leaf recording eleven scholars and that no leave was asked for the room because none was thought likely to be given.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The Leòid circuit in the north

told_in.section: V. Of the Second School and the Minute Copied Fair

events.title: Daniel Frayne walks in from Muileann leathan
events.body: A fisherman's son of ten walks the coast path each morning from Muileann leathan to sit on Agnes Pike's benches, and back again in time to help haul his father's nets, a condition he keeps every day the school runs that winter.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Agnes Pike's school

told_in.section: III. Of Daniel Frayne

events.title: Daniel Frayne's fair copies pinned to the byre wall
events.body: Slower at reading than at writing, the boy is set to copy out each day's psalm or minute a second time, and by the spring his fair copies, stroke for stroke exact, are pinned the length of the byre's one dry wall.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The Leòid circuit in the north

told_in.section: III. Of Daniel Frayne

events.title: The maor visits the byre school and writes nothing
events.body: The shire's maor, whose office is to note anything newly opened in it, rides out, watches the children recite a psalm, asks Agnes Pike only after the room's heating and the children's fees, and sends south that season a report of harvest, head-due and bridge that says nothing of the school at all.

links.label: At the same time
links.title: Agnes Pike's school

told_in.section: IV. Of the Maor Who Wrote Nothing

events.title: Alice Hale opens a second school at Caol mhòr
events.body: Walter Hale's daughter Alice opens a school of her own in a disused net-store behind the harbour at Caol mhòr, on a purse thinner than her father carried north, and writes to Agnes Pike asking what has answered best on the byre's cold mornings.

links.label: At the same time
links.title: Agnes Pike's school

told_in.section: V. Of the Second School and the Minute Copied Fair

events.title: The Cill ghlas fault line walked and found unmoved
events.body: Lachlann mac Iain Bhàin and his chainman Iain mac Ruairidh trace the old Cill ghlas fault foot by foot with plumb and cord and file a report at Cathair mhòr declaring the district safe to work again so long as new shafts are cut a full chain back from it.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The Cill ghlas district reopened

told_in.section: V. Of the Second School and the Minute Copied Fair

events.title: The school moves to the church porch for summer
events.body: With the widow's cattle wanting the byre back for the warm months, Agnes Pike's school moves into the porch of the Doire ghlas church, a change it makes every summer after.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The Leòid circuit in the north

told_in.section: V. Of the Second School and the Minute Copied Fair

events.title: Daniel Frayne copies the minute of the school's own founding
events.body: On the last morning before the move to the church porch, Agnes Pike sets her best copyist Tional nan Tuathach's own four-line minute recording the school's opening, and pins his fair copy into the register's first leaf rather than to the drying wall.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The Leòid circuit in the north

told_in.section: V. Of the Second School and the Minute Copied Fair

events.title: Eilidh nic Leòid opens the Ceann mhòr assize
events.body: In the heat of an t-Iuchar, with the windows of the old magistrate's house propped open against the fish-yard smell, Eilidh nic Leòid tells the crowded room that she will hear all nineteen causes on the list to their own ends, in their own order, whatever the likeness of one paper to the next, and whatever the weather asks of everyone waiting on the bench.

links.label: Same place
links.title: The Leòid circuit in the north

told_in.section: I. Of the Court in the Heat

events.title: The Dunlop title read to its end
events.body: Eilidh nic Leòid reads a human grant brown at its folds, and a receipt for seed corn the family thought to bring unasked, and finds as she found seven years before at Seann Bhral: the ground is An Crùn's, the working of it the Dunlops', on the same terms as before and no excusal from any due to come.

links.label: Same place
links.title: The Leòid circuit in the north

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The Leòid ruling

told_in.section: II. Of the Papers Brown at the Fold

events.title: Fifteen suits found for An Crùn at Ceann mhòr
events.body: Cause after cause of the seventeen brought on human titles is decided in the words of Breith Leòid, the ground passing to An Crùn and the working of it staying with the family that holds it, until the room has learned, before the week is out, to stop guessing at an ending it already knows.

links.label: Same place
links.title: The Leòid circuit in the north

told_in.section: III. Of the Two Found for the Holders

events.title: A custodian's countersign found on the Coombe title
events.body: In the margin of a Tuathaich family's human grant, Eilidh nic Leòid finds the pressed mark of an old land-keeping custodian, witness to the transfer in the humans' own time, and rules that a grant allowed also by an office of the island's own older law stands on ground the closing of An t-Aiseag never touched.

links.label: Same place
links.title: The Leòid circuit in the north

told_in.section: III. Of the Two Found for the Holders

events.title: The Coombes and the Pettifers found for the holders
events.body: Two of the seventeen suits at Ceann mhòr, each carrying a custodian's old countersign on its title, are found whole for the families that hold them, the only two of the assize's nineteen causes decided against An Crùn that summer.

links.label: Same place
links.title: The Leòid circuit in the north

told_in.section: V. Of the Inn at Ceann mhòr

events.title: Walter Hale heard as a witness at Ceann mhòr
events.body: Having no standing to plead, Walter Hale is called instead to the bench as a witness, and shows Eilidh nic Leòid Tional nan Tuathach's own minute of a family's land divided by agreement and set down in writing years before, which the court accepts over the memory of the parties themselves.

links.label: Same place
links.title: The Leòid circuit in the north

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The Moot's schoolhouse petition

told_in.section: IV. Of the Witness Heard

events.title: Tional nan Tuathach's minute-books credited by a Crown bench
events.body: Eilidh nic Leòid rules that a record kept by a body An Crùn does not recognise is no less a fact for the hand that wrote it holding no seal, the first time Tional nan Tuathach's own paper is taken as evidence before a circuit justice.

links.label: Same place
links.title: The Leòid circuit in the north

told_in.section: VI. Of the Road Home and the Book

events.title: Hale and Eilidh nic Leòid speak at the Ceann mhòr inn
events.body: Over supper Walter Hale asks Eilidh nic Leòid whether an exact law can also be a fair one; she tells him plainly that she made her ruling to be exact rather than kind, and that she knows whose convenience it was written to serve, a thing she has told no maor and no council chest.

links.label: Same place
links.title: The Leòid circuit in the north

told_in.section: V. Of the Inn at Ceann mhòr

events.title: Eilidh nic Leòid begins the gathered book
events.body: Through the winter after the Ceann mhòr sitting, Eilidh nic Leòid sets down in one book the whole of her nine years' rulings on Tuathaich land, from Breith Seann Bhral to the seventeen suits, so that a justice after her need not dig the council's own chests to learn what she already knows.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Eilidh nic Leòid dies

told_in.section: VI. Of the Road Home and the Book

events.title: Eilidh nic Leòid at the Seann Bhral harbour wall
events.body: Riding on from Àth leathan by the western road after the Ceann mhòr assize, Eilidh nic Leòid stands a while before the light fails at the harbour wall of Seann Bhral in the west, where she gave Breith Leòid seven years before, and says nothing of it to Murchadh Clàrc.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The Leòid circuit in the north

told_in.section: VI. Of the Road Home and the Book

events.title: Eilidh nic Leòid dies
events.body: Eilidh nic Leòid dies at Cathair dhomhain. Her rulings are bound in one book, the first law-book of the restored kingdom, and every circuit justice after her carries a copy.

links.label: Caused by
links.title: Eilidh nic Leòid begins the gathered book

links.label: Caused by
links.title: Eilidh nic Leòid sends for Uilleam mac Leòid

links.label: Same place
links.title: Eilidh nic Leòid dies at Cathair dhomhain

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Leabhar nam Breith bound

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Uilleam mac Leòid named to the northern circuit

events.title: Eilidh nic Leòid sends for Uilleam mac Leòid
events.body: Failing through am Màrt, Eilidh nic Leòid sends word north to her brother's son Uilleam, a young man who has ridden the northern circuit with her twice as a boy, asking him to take up the circuit she can no longer ride.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Eilidh nic Leòid dies

told_in.section: VI. Of the Road Home and the Book

events.title: Eilidh nic Leòid dies at Cathair dhomhain
events.body: Eilidh nic Leòid dies in her own house within sound of the harbour, her clerk Murchadh Clàrc beside her and the gathered book of her rulings finished but not yet bound on the table by the bed.

links.label: Same place
links.title: Eilidh nic Leòid dies

told_in.section: VI. Of the Road Home and the Book

events.title: Leabhar nam Breith bound
events.body: The council's own binder binds Eilidh nic Leòid's gathered rulings in plain calf under the name she chose for it herself, Leabhar nam Breith, and every circuit justice after her is given a copy to carry.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Eilidh nic Leòid dies

told_in.section: VI. Of the Road Home and the Book

events.title: Uilleam mac Leòid named to the northern circuit
events.body: Uilleam mac Leòid is named circuit justice of the north in his aunt's place, and rides for his first assize with Leabhar nam Breith strapped behind his clerk's saddle, as the satchel of blank record-books was once strapped behind his aunt's.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Eilidh nic Leòid dies

told_in.section: VI. Of the Road Home and the Book

events.title: Leabharlann Muileann chaol founded
events.body: A great library is founded at Muileann chaol. In time it holds the fullest record of the island's past that has come down.

events.title: Ailean Leabhar, first keeper
events.body: Ailean mac Iain, called Ailean Leabhar, is made the first keeper of Leabharlann Muileann chaol. He brings with him the council's minute-books and what is left of the humans' tithe ledgers, takes in the custodians' rolls kept in the town's cellars since the Severance war, and spends his first years having them read.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Ailean mac Iain named first keeper of the Library

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The custodians' rolls found under Muileann chaol

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The council's minute-books sent east to an Leabharlann

links.label: Leads to
links.title: An Leabharlann's copyists turn every date to the civil calendar

links.label: Leads to
links.title: An Aois Ailein parted from the eldest age

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill sent to inspect Leabharlann Muileann chaol

events.title: A chur san Leabharlann
events.body: Within a few years 'a chur san Leabharlann', to put it in the Library, is said of anything settled beyond dispute. Ailean Leabhar is said to have disliked the phrase, for the Library settles nothing, he said, and only keeps.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Coinneach Clàrc taken on at an Leabharlann

links.label: Leads to
links.title: "A chur san Leabharlann" first said at Muileann chaol

events.title: Ailean mac Iain named first keeper of the Library
events.body: By the council's own sentence, Ailean mac Iain is named keeper of the record at Muileann chaol, to receive, to order, and to keep whatever is sent to him. The office has no precedent and the warrant no further words, leaving Ailean to learn from the town itself what a keeper of a record might be.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Ailean Leabhar, first keeper

told_in.book: Of the Cellar at Muileann chaol
told_in.section: I. Of the Cellar Under the Stair

events.title: The custodians' rolls found under Muileann chaol
events.body: The town's own custodians lead Ailean Leabhar down a stair to a wet cellar under the old grain-store, where rolls and bound books have stood on planks above standing water since before An Dealachadh, the lowest tier gone soft as bread. He reads three lines by the light thrown down the stair, then sends for lamps and a table.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Ailean Leabhar, first keeper

told_in.book: Of the Cellar at Muileann chaol
told_in.section: I. Of the Cellar Under the Stair

events.title: Coinneach Clàrc taken on at an Leabharlann
events.body: A wright's orphaned son of Muileann chaol, thirteen that spring and hired out by his mother for whatever a household could spare, attaches himself to Ailean Leabhar's carts on their first afternoon in the town and is set to fetch and carry, and within the year to read a Mission hand that few south of the guard-line can any longer make out.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: A chur san Leabharlann

told_in.book: Of the Cellar at Muileann chaol
told_in.section: I. Of the Cellar Under the Stair

events.title: The council's minute-books sent east to an Leabharlann
events.body: Four sacks of the council's own minute-books, and behind them the boxed and charred tithe ledgers of the humans' counting-houses that Ailean boxed unread fourteen years before, are carried east from Cathair dhearg to Muileann chaol, the first of the kingdom's scattered papers to be gathered into one keeping.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Ailean Leabhar, first keeper

told_in.book: Of the Cellar at Muileann chaol
told_in.section: II. Of the Long Reading

events.title: An Leabharlann's first reading room opened
events.body: Ailean Leabhar opens a dry chamber above the cellar to any who can show a letter from a shire maor vouching for their errand, on the plain reasoning that a Library nobody can reach is no better kept than a cellar nobody can reach. For the better part of a year it stands empty of anyone but his own copyists.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The first readers

told_in.book: Of the Cellar at Muileann chaol
told_in.section: IV. Of the First Readers

events.title: The first readers
events.body: The library's first reading room is opened to any who can show a letter from a shire maor. The first reader written in its book is a shipwright of Ros dhomhain, who asks for the humans' plans of their hulls.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: An Leabharlann's first reading room opened

links.label: Leads to
links.title: A Ros dhomhain shipwright first signs the reading-book

events.title: The bath-house at the hot springs
events.body: A new bath-house is built over the hot springs near Muileann ruadh, paid for by the Guild of Hewers for miners sick with the dust. The guild's sick-roll for its first year names four hundred men by name and shift.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Comann nan Gualadairean' bath-house built at Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh

events.title: The keepers of the five lights
events.body: The five lighthouses built under the humans are given Dia-thìrich keepers by royal warrant. At Taigh-solais Baile chrom on the Tuathaich coast the keeper is a Dia-thìreach man lodged in a Tuathaich town, and his warrant bids him report what he sees on land as well as at sea.

links.label: Caused by
links.title: The keeper's report pinned at Caol mhòr

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The five lighthouses given Dia-thìreach keepers

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The keeper's light lit at Baile chrom

events.title: The Muileann chaol town grows
events.body: Copyists, binders and paper-makers settle at Muileann chaol about the library. The town is granted a market charter, and its first market day is held in the library's yard.

links.label: Same place
links.title: The fuel burned at the Muileann chaol market

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Cailean mac Eachainn's Sloinneadh Aisling found in the margin

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Leabhar nan Sloinnidhean opened

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Leabhar nan Aithrisean opened

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The market entered in an Leabharlann's register

links.label: Caused by
links.title: Muileann chaol granted a market charter

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The first market day held in an Leabharlann's yard

events.title: An Leabharlann's copyists turn every date to the civil calendar
events.body: Ailean Leabhar sets his copyists to turning every date the cellar and the tithe ledgers hold into the civil calendar the humans brought, disliking the old count of An Diosal, which runs backward into the thousands and names every year after the day the humans' kin went over the water.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Ailean Leabhar, first keeper

told_in.book: Of the Cellar at Muileann chaol
told_in.section: II. Of the Long Reading

events.title: An Aois Ailein parted from the eldest age
events.body: Laying the tellings of Clann na Ceiste against Clàr nan Rìghrean the custodians' rolls preserve, Ailean Leabhar's reckoners find that nearly half of the copyists' eldest age falls within the single life of Ailean Mòr, and by the consent of all seven copyists that life is counted an age of its own, the first change an Leabharlann makes to any reckoning it did not itself invent.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Ailean Leabhar, first keeper

told_in.book: Of the Cellar at Muileann chaol
told_in.section: II. Of the Long Reading

events.title: "A chur san Leabharlann" first said at Muileann chaol
events.body: A council clerk, told that a boundary query will want weeks of reading before it can be honestly answered, says the matter can simply be put in an Leabharlann and left settled. Ailean Leabhar corrects him sharply, and the correction, carried home and retold, is what fixes the phrase in the town's mouth rather than loosening it.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: A chur san Leabharlann

told_in.book: Of the Cellar at Muileann chaol
told_in.section: II. Of the Long Reading

events.title: Cailean mac Eachainn's Sloinneadh Aisling found in the margin
events.body: Copying a camp roll of Àth ìseal a third time, Coinneach Clàrc notices a second, later hand in its margin: Cailean mac Eachainn's line of descent, Sloinneadh Aisling, set down a great many years before. Ailean Leabhar has it copied fair within the week.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The Muileann chaol town grows

told_in.book: Of the Cellar at Muileann chaol
told_in.section: III. Of the Two Books

events.title: Leabhar nan Sloinnidhean opened
events.body: Ailean Leabhar begins a book for nothing but lines of descent, naming it Leabhar nan Sloinnidhean, and sets Cailean mac Eachainn's Sloinneadh Aisling in it directly after the older Sloinneadh a' Chlachair, found wedged behind a shifted course of brick in the same cellar.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The Muileann chaol town grows

told_in.book: Of the Cellar at Muileann chaol
told_in.section: III. Of the Two Books

events.title: Leabhar nan Aithrisean opened
events.body: Where the Àth ìseal roll's margin also keeps tales set down by firelight rather than by day, Marbh-bheò, the white stag, a captain's boast of a wolf and a door held alone, Ailean Leabhar opens a second book, Leabhar nan Aithrisean, and enters na Bliadhnachan Fada of Ailean Mòr and his children beside them without correction.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The Muileann chaol town grows

told_in.book: Of the Cellar at Muileann chaol
told_in.section: III. Of the Two Books

events.title: A Ros dhomhain shipwright first signs the reading-book
events.body: A shipwright of Ros dhomhain walks the coast road with a maor's letter to ask whether the humans ever set down the true lines of a hull. Ailean Leabhar finds three drawings folded inside an unrelated survey, and the shipwright copies them out over four days, the first name entered in an Leabharlann's reading-book.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The first readers

told_in.book: Of the Cellar at Muileann chaol
told_in.section: IV. Of the First Readers

events.title: Comann nan Gualadairean' bath-house built at Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh
events.body: Comann nan Gualadairean builds a bath-house of its own funds over Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh below Muileann ruadh, for men the pits have made sick with the dust, and sends an Leabharlann its first sick-roll unasked: four hundred men named by shift and by face of the pit that broke them.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The bath-house at the hot springs

told_in.book: Of the Cellar at Muileann chaol
told_in.section: IV. Of the First Readers

events.title: The five lighthouses given Dia-thìreach keepers
events.body: By royal warrant the five lighthouses built under the humans are given keepers of the kingdom's own naming. Ailean Leabhar drafts all five, the four southern warrants alike and the fifth, for Baile chrom on the Tuathaich coast, bidding its keeper report what he sees by land as well as by sea.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The keepers of the five lights

told_in.book: Of the Cellar at Muileann chaol
told_in.section: VI. Of the Five Lights

events.title: The keeper's light lit at Baile chrom
events.body: A Dia-thìreach keeper who asked for the northern posting himself takes up the light at Baile chrom, among a Tuathaich town that has never before had a Dia-thìreach man set to live and watch among it. The southern four lights draw no comment; the fifth draws only silence that first season.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The keepers of the five lights

told_in.book: Of the Cellar at Muileann chaol
told_in.section: VI. Of the Five Lights

events.title: The market entered in an Leabharlann's register
events.body: Ailean Leabhar enters the market granted to Muileann chaol in an Leabharlann's own register, its stall-fee a penny a table and its first court kept by a wright's widow with a length of string, the first entry in that book to concern the town rather than the record.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The Muileann chaol town grows

told_in.book: Of the Cellar at Muileann chaol
told_in.section: V. Of the Market in the Yard

events.title: Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill sent to inspect Leabharlann Muileann chaol
events.body: The council sends its under-clerk Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill, four-and-forty, to see and report on the record Ailean Leabhar has kept at Muileann chaol since its founding, the errand falling to her only for want of causes on her own desk that month.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Ailean Leabhar, first keeper

told_in.book: Of the Table of the Ages
told_in.section: I. Of the Errand to Muileann chaol

events.title: Muileann chaol granted a market charter
events.body: The district's maor writes up, at the keeper's own asking, that a town which has drawn copyists, binders and paper-makers to it in two years without leave might as well be given a charter before its own trade sets its rules instead. The council grants it in the usual form, a fee for every stall and a court to hear the fair's disputes.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The Muileann chaol town grows

told_in.book: Of the Table of the Ages
told_in.section: II. Of the Report Nobody Above Her Would Read

events.title: The first market day held in an Leabharlann's yard
events.body: Thirty stalls of thread, nails, candles and the district's own produce are set up on trestles against an Leabharlann's wall, the stall-fee a penny a table paid into a box the keeper's boy carries, and the fair's own court amounting to the boy's mother settling disputes over table-space in a voice heard the length of the yard.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The Muileann chaol town grows

told_in.book: Of the Table of the Ages
told_in.section: II. Of the Report Nobody Above Her Would Read

events.title: The Tobar dhìreach mill's first delivery reaches an Leabharlann
events.body: Forty quires of the new paper-mill's paper are carried up the road on a borrowed cart, better and cheaper, by the copyists' own judgement, than anything the council's stationers at Cathair dhearg have sent north; within the year near enough every sheet an Leabharlann uses comes from the one stream.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The paper-mill at Tobar dhìreach

told_in.book: Of the Table of the Ages
told_in.section: II. Of the Report Nobody Above Her Would Read

events.title: The paper-mill at Tobar dhìreach
events.body: A paper-mill is built at Tobar dhìreach, a few miles from the library, on the stream below the village. For half a century nearly every page of the royal chronicle is written on its paper.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The Tobar dhìreach mill's first delivery reaches an Leabharlann

events.title: The first royal chronicler appointed
events.body: An office is made to keep the records of the kingdom. From it comes the archive whence these annals are drawn.

links.label: Same place
links.title: The office of royal chronicler set at Muileann chaol, not the capital

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Gormshuil sworn royal chronicler

events.title: The years counted by the ages
events.body: With the office of chronicler the council orders that the kingdom's records shall count their years no longer by the Diosal but by the ages of the library's table, each age from its own first event: six ages as the table then stands, and seven since the Dubhan Era. The chronicler's first year is entered as the eighteenth of the Severance Era. Thereafter the count of the Diosal is kept only in old books.

events.title: Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill
events.body: The first royal chronicler is Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill, a clerk of the council. She keeps her record at Muileann chaol and not at the capital, and writes in her first entry that a record kept beside the throne is kept for the throne.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The office of royal chronicler set at Muileann chaol, not the capital

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Uilleam mac Griogair names the under-clerk

events.title: The office of royal chronicler set at Muileann chaol, not the capital
events.body: Sworn into the new office at Cathair dhearg and given no instruction as to its seat, Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill writes back within the week that she means to keep the record at Muileann chaol, beside an Leabharlann that already holds the rolls and the copyists the work wants, and that a record kept beside the throne is kept for the throne.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill

links.label: Same place
links.title: The first royal chronicler appointed

told_in.book: Of the Table of the Ages
told_in.section: III. Of the Office Made

events.title: Gormshuil sworn royal chronicler
events.body: Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill is sworn royal chronicler in a small room at Cathair dhearg on the twentieth of an t-Samhain, four-and-forty, before a clerk who reads the warrant's clause on the counting of the years in the same flat voice as its clause on her seat.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The first royal chronicler appointed

told_in.book: Of the Table of the Ages
told_in.section: III. Of the Office Made

events.title: Uilleam mac Griogair names the under-clerk
events.body: When the office of chronicler is made, it is Uilleam mac Griogair, clerk of council, who remembers that the under-clerk he sent to Muileann chaol came back with more to say than he had troubled to hear, and names her to it.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill

told_in.book: Of the Table of the Ages
told_in.section: III. Of the Office Made

events.title: The first chronicle circuit
events.body: Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill sends clerks to every shire to copy parish books, grave-lists and harbour rolls. The returns from the south fill forty chests. The returns from Siorrachd Àth àrsaidh and the other northern shires fill one, for few Tuathaich will speak to the clerks.

links.label: Same person
links.title: Tormod mac Sheumais joins the first chronicle circuit

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The town arms of five hundred and five burghs copied into one book

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Eachdraidh na Rìoghachd clerks turned away at Doire ghlas

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The northern chest opened: the maor's returns and nothing more

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Eachdraidh na Rìoghachd clerks ride out in three pairs

events.title: The town arms copied
events.body: The clerks of the first chronicle circuit copy the seal of every town they visit into the roll of arms, and the roll comes to hold the arms of five hundred and five places. In the north most are copied from the humans' old town seals, for few Tuathaich will show the clerks their own.

events.title: The chest from Inis bheag
events.body: At Inis bheag in the north-east the chronicle clerks are shown a parish book that goes back before the coming of the humans, kept in the Seann Spioradan house there. The keeper lets it be copied, and not taken.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The Inis bheag keeper lets his parish book be copied and not carried

events.title: Boats lost off Cuan bheag
events.body: A storm out of the west drowns eleven Tuathaich fishermen off Cuan bheag in the north. The village has no lifeboat. The Moot buys one by subscription and asks the council to pay half; the council pays a third.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Thomas Coyle drowned off Cuan bheag

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Mary Coyle's roll of the eleven dead

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Tional nan Tuathach opens its lifeboat subscription

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The eleven stones set at Cuan bheag

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The Cuan bheag lifeboat launched

events.title: Tormod mac Sheumais joins the first chronicle circuit
events.body: A council under-clerk's son of three-and-thirty, called already Tormod Pinn for the speed of his hand, asks Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill for a place on the first circuit rather than wait to be sent, and rides the northern half of it.

links.label: Same person
links.title: The first chronicle circuit

told_in.book: Of the Table of the Ages
told_in.section: IV. Of the First Circuit

events.title: The town arms of five hundred and five burghs copied into one book
events.body: Eachdraidh na Rìoghachd circuit's southern chests yield the town arms of every burgh that has ever cut a seal, five hundred and five of them, entered by Coinneach Clàrc in the order the chests happen to arrive rather than by rank, on Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill's own ruling that a tidied record forgets how untidy its own arrival was.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The first chronicle circuit

told_in.book: Of the Table of the Ages
told_in.section: IV. Of the First Circuit

events.title: Eachdraidh na Rìoghachd clerks turned away at Doire ghlas
events.body: Tormod mac Sheumais reads the circuit's own warrant twice aloud in the street at the harbour agent's demand before he is let copy a single ledger; eleven of the town's twelve doors stay closed against him, an answer he judges memory rather than unkindness.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The first chronicle circuit

told_in.book: Of the Table of the Ages
told_in.section: V. Of the Door at Doire ghlas

events.title: The Inis bheag keeper lets his parish book be copied and not carried
events.body: The old keeper of Na Seann Spioradan house at Inis bheag hears the circuit's warrant once, without asking it twice, and lets his parish roll be copied at his own table under his own eye, but will not let the book itself travel so much as to the harbour, telling the clerk that a book kept that many generations belongs to the house and not to any seal.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The chest from Inis bheag

told_in.book: Of the Table of the Ages
told_in.section: VI. Of the Chest from Inis bheag

events.title: The northern chest opened: the maor's returns and nothing more
events.body: Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill opens the one chest the northern shires have filled and finds only the maor of Siorrachd Àth àrsaidh's own tallies and licences, not a line in it written by a Tuathaich hand; she enters the fact plainly and adds no further word to it.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The first chronicle circuit

told_in.book: Of the Table of the Ages
told_in.section: VI. Of the Chest from Inis bheag

events.title: Eachdraidh na Rìoghachd clerks ride out in three pairs
events.body: In the spring the first chronicle circuit's clerks ride out in three pairs, one south, one to the eastern shires nearer the mountain and one north past Cnoc ghorm to the Tuathaich coast, each pair with its own warrant and its own chest to fill.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The first chronicle circuit

told_in.book: Of the Table of the Ages
told_in.section: IV. Of the First Circuit

events.title: Thomas Coyle drowned off Cuan bheag
events.body: A westerly storm on the second night of an t-Sultain drowns eleven Tuathaich fishermen out of Cuan bheag, Thomas Coyle of Caol mhòr among them, one-and-forty and near twenty years married to Mary Coyle. The sea gives back two broken hulls and a stranger's oar; the town buries what it can within the week.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Boats lost off Cuan bheag

told_in.section: I. Of the Boats Lost off Cuan bheag

events.title: Mary Coyle's roll of the eleven dead
events.body: Mary Coyle, newly widowed, writes the eleven drowned men's names out on a single sheet for the mason's stones, setting them in the order the boats went out rather than the order the sea gave the bodies back, holding that order the truer one.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Boats lost off Cuan bheag

told_in.section: I. Of the Boats Lost off Cuan bheag

events.title: Tional nan Tuathach opens its lifeboat subscription
events.body: Walter Hale carries the wreck's news to Tional nan Tuathach's own council at Caol mhòr, which votes that same evening to open a subscription for a lifeboat at Cuan bheag; Hale opens the list himself, and it carries near two hundred names by the month's end. The council, asked to bear half the cost, answers four months on that it will bear a third.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Boats lost off Cuan bheag

told_in.section: I. Of the Boats Lost off Cuan bheag

events.title: The tale of Uilebheist na Mara told to the chronicler
