events.body: A fisherman out of Achadh àrsaidh, at the summer bothies below the cold cape, tells Seanchaidh na Rìoghachd Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill the coast's own tale of a shape seen off the cold cape, seen always at a distance and never named by those who fear it, which she enters in the book that keeps what people said rather than the book that keeps names.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The thing off the north-west cape

told_in.section: II. Of the Thing off the Cape

events.title: The raiders' anchorage noted at the cold cape
events.body: The same fisherman tells Gormshuil that Na Longan gun Bhratach working those waters know the cold cape's currents better than any stranger crew should, and keep some hidden anchorage among its rocks; she writes it apart from the tale and asks that the council's coastal watch be told of it.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The thing off the north-west cape

told_in.section: II. Of the Thing off the Cape

events.title: The flocks of Eilean dhubh counted by their own hands
events.body: A treasury clerk sent to number the flocks of Eilean dhubh for the head-due finds the islanders unwilling to have him count their own pastures, and takes instead their sworn count by tally-stick, on which the island's dues are set that year and every year after.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The Eilean dhubh sheep-count

told_in.section: III. Of the Flocks Counted and the Two Requests

events.title: The eleven stones set at Cuan bheag
events.body: The mason of Cuan bheag cuts and sets eleven stones for the drowned from Mary Coyle's single sheet, in the order the boats went out, and they stand weathering by the jetty when the lifeboat is put into the water the spring after.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Boats lost off Cuan bheag

told_in.section: I. Of the Boats Lost off Cuan bheag

events.title: The thing off the north-west cape
events.body: Fishermen out of Achadh àrsaidh tell of a creature longer than their boats in the waters off the north-west cape. Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill writes down the tale, and adds that the raiders shelter in those same waters.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The tale of Uilebheist na Mara told to the chronicler

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The raiders' anchorage noted at the cold cape

events.title: The Eilean dhubh sheep-count
events.body: A royal clerk is sent to count the flocks of Eilean dhubh, greatest of the outer isles, to set the island's dues. The islanders count them for him, and the dues are set on their count.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The flocks of Eilean dhubh counted by their own hands

events.title: Cathair gheal arms its boats
events.body: The Tuathaich fishermen of Cathair gheal arm their own boats and drive the raiders from the bay. Twice they had asked the council for help, and none was sent. Afterwards the council fines the town for bearing arms without licence, and the fine is paid.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Nell Barrow's first letter for Cathair gheal

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Nell Barrow's second letter for Cathair gheal

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The black ship run aground in Cathair gheal's bay

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Two dead and four hurt in the bay's clearing

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Cathair gheal fined for bearing arms unlicensed

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Walter Hale carries Tional nan Tuathach's purse north to Cathair gheal

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The fine paid at the maor's door

events.title: The market cross at Cathair mhòr
events.body: A market cross is raised at Cathair mhòr at the cost of the house of Mac Ùisdein, with the house's name cut on all four faces. The town's wool and coal markets are moved to its foot.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Ellen Hale dies at Caol mhòr

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Ellen Hale buried on the rise above the harbour

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Crosses and lifeboats

events.title: The Cuan bheag lifeboat launched
events.body: The lifeboat ordered of the Cuan shean yard comes up the coast in an Cèitean and is set afloat off Cuan bheag's jetty by the hands of that autumn's five widows, no priest of either faith having an agreed form to bless a boat neither had built.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Boats lost off Cuan bheag

told_in.section: I. Of the Boats Lost off Cuan bheag

events.title: Nell Barrow's first letter for Cathair gheal
events.body: Nell Barrow, a skipper's widow of Cathair gheal who has lost a nephew to the raiders, writes the town's case to the council in am Faoilleach, asking a boat armed at the council's expense or leave to arm the town's own; the maor warns her plain words are as likely filed as answered. No answer comes.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Cathair gheal arms its boats

told_in.section: III. Of the Flocks Counted and the Two Requests

events.title: Nell Barrow's second letter for Cathair gheal
events.body: Two months unanswered, Nell Barrow writes a second letter in am Màrt, shorter and plainer than the first, ending that the town does not think a third asking will find the council less occupied than the first two were. It too goes unanswered.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Cathair gheal arms its boats

told_in.section: III. Of the Flocks Counted and the Two Requests

events.title: The black ship run aground in Cathair gheal's bay
events.body: On the night of 8 an Giblean three flagless hulls stand into Cathair gheal's bay; the largest raider ship runs her keel onto a shifted bar and is boarded and burned by seven town boats before dawn, the two lesser hulls standing off rather than come to her aid.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Cathair gheal arms its boats

told_in.section: IV. Of the Bay Cleared

events.title: Two dead and four hurt in the bay's clearing
events.body: The fight for Cathair gheal's bay costs the town two men dead and four hurt, one of whom keeps no further use of a hand; Nell Barrow herself takes a burn from a fallen lantern that scars her the rest of her life, and by first light tells the town the bay is clear.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Cathair gheal arms its boats

told_in.section: IV. Of the Bay Cleared

events.title: Cathair gheal fined for bearing arms unlicensed
events.body: The council's ruling on the night's fight names no boat sent and no licence granted, only that Cathair gheal bore arms without leave first asked, and fines the town four purses of Bonn na Rìoghachd, to be paid at the maor's own office before the year's dues fall due.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Cathair gheal arms its boats

told_in.section: V. Of the Fine Paid

events.title: Walter Hale carries Tional nan Tuathach's purse north to Cathair gheal
events.body: Hearing the town lacks two-thirds of its fine, Walter Hale carries the difference north from Tional nan Tuathach's own purse, the same purse the Cuan bheag lifeboat has already thinned, and reaches Cathair gheal near the end of an t-Iuchar.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Cathair gheal arms its boats

told_in.section: V. Of the Fine Paid

events.title: The fine paid at the maor's door
events.body: Nell Barrow's sum and Hale's together clear the fine in full at the maor's own door, counted coin by coin before his clerk, who enters the sum received and asks nothing of the six years, the two letters, or the boat the town was never sent.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Cathair gheal arms its boats

told_in.section: V. Of the Fine Paid

events.title: Ellen Hale dies at Caol mhòr
events.body: Ellen Hale, Walter Hale's wife, dies at Caol mhòr in the second week of an Lùnastal at seventy, in the loft the family had lodged in since the boat brought them north; Tional nan Tuathach's day-book gives the day and the hour, and beneath them David's line that Tional nan Tuathach did not sit that week.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The market cross at Cathair mhòr

told_in.section: VI. Of Ellen Hale

events.title: Ellen Hale buried on the rise above the harbour
events.body: Ellen Hale is buried on the rise above Caol mhòr's harbour with the fishwives, the Carrick women, the widows of the Cuan bheag drowning and the whole of Tional nan Tuathach's council standing by; the minister reads the twenty-third psalm, from which she had taught her children their letters, and her husband says nothing aloud.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The market cross at Cathair mhòr

told_in.section: VI. Of Ellen Hale

events.title: Crosses and lifeboats
events.body: Hearing the council's long minute on the Mac Ùisdein market cross read at Tional nan Tuathach's table beside its short one on Cathair gheal's fine, Mary Coyle says that the council seems to know a great deal about crosses and rather less about lifeboats, and goes back to counting the boats home.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The market cross at Cathair mhòr

told_in.section: V. Of the Fine Paid

events.title: The house of the Stone at Caol leathan
events.body: The house of Òrd na Cloiche at Caol leathan, greatest of the order, is rebuilt with a tower, and a bell rings the hours from it. The town sets its market and its courts by the bell.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Lia Fàil's house at Caol leathan rebuilt

events.title: Fèill Muileann òg first held
events.body: A fair is held each year at Muileann òg, and it becomes the greatest gathering on the island. Trade comes to it from every province the state holds.

links.label: Caused by
links.title: The coal-sellers' row stands empty at the fair

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The fair-field marked out at Muileann òg

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Cùirt na Fèille roofed

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Cùirt na Fèille's first sitting

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The spoil-stone case judged by a smith's eye

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The first fair runs a fortnight

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Pipers from Baile chiar at the first fair

events.title: Oighrig nic Mhathain's rules
events.body: Oighrig nic Mhathain, first toll-mistress of the fair at Muileann òg, sets its rules: a stall-fee in coin, a court of the fair for disputes, and Tuathaich goods to be sold only through Dia-thìrich factors. The rules are read aloud at the opening of every fair to this day.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Oighrig nic Mhathain named toll-mistress

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Oighrig writes the fair's three rules

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The first factors licensed for northern goods

links.label: Leads to
links.title: David Hale's wool turned away at the gate

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Tional nan Tuathach's letter against the factor rule filed

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The fair's rules confirmed and read aloud

events.title: The fair's road
events.body: The road from Cathair dhearg to Muileann òg is widened and metalled for the carts of the fair. It passes Dùn chrom, which takes a toll at its gate and grows on it. As far as Muileann ghlas it runs on the old coal road; the new stretches are called Rathad na Fèille.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The fair's road metalled past Dùn chrom

events.title: Lia Fàil's house at Caol leathan rebuilt
events.body: Òrd na Cloiche rebuilds its house at Caol leathan at its own cost, raising a bell tower over the western gable; the town sets its market and its two courts by the bell from that year on.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The house of the Stone at Caol leathan

told_in.book: Of the Fair at Muileann òg
told_in.section: I. Of the Bell at Caol leathan

events.title: Oighrig nic Mhathain named toll-mistress
events.body: Oighrig nic Mhathain, nine years the market clerk of Dùn chrom and one-and-thirty that year, is asked by the council's eastern factor to keep the new fair to be held at the ford by Muileann òg, and takes the post, leaving her own scales to a niece she has trained two summers at her elbow.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Oighrig nic Mhathain's rules

told_in.book: Of the Fair at Muileann òg
told_in.section: II. Of Oighrig, Market Clerk of Dùn chrom

events.title: The fair-field marked out at Muileann òg
events.body: Oighrig nic Mhathain walks the ground at Muileann òg with a length of cord and a stick through the summer, marking the stalls, the beast-pens and the corner where a court might sit, before any building has been raised there.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Fèill Muileann òg first held

told_in.book: Of the Fair at Muileann òg
told_in.section: II. Of Oighrig, Market Clerk of Dùn chrom

events.title: Cùirt na Fèille roofed
events.body: Carpenters of Dùn chrom finish a plain roofed frame, open on three sides, at the field's corner nearest the ford, a fortnight before the fair is to open; it is the only building the state gives the fair in its first year.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Fèill Muileann òg first held

told_in.book: Of the Fair at Muileann òg
told_in.section: II. Of Oighrig, Market Clerk of Dùn chrom

events.title: Oighrig writes the fair's three rules
events.body: Over three evenings by rush-light Oighrig nic Mhathain writes the fair's rules in her own plain hand: a stall-fee in coin, a court of the fair to sit each day of the gathering, and Tuathaich goods to be sold only through licensed Dia-thìreach factors, on the council's own instruction.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Oighrig nic Mhathain's rules

told_in.book: Of the Fair at Muileann òg
told_in.section: III. Of the Rules Written in Her Own Hand

events.title: The first factors licensed for northern goods
events.body: The council licenses four merchant houses of the eastern shires to stand factors' stalls at Muileann òg and sell Tuathaich goods under their own names for a share of the price; Oighrig nic Mhathain enters their names under a heading of her own, Bàillidhean na Fèille.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Oighrig nic Mhathain's rules

told_in.book: Of the Fair at Muileann òg
told_in.section: III. Of the Rules Written in Her Own Hand

events.title: Cùirt na Fèille's first sitting
events.body: On the fair's opening morning, 16 an Dàmhair, Oighrig nic Mhathain's court hears its first case, a dispute over a barrel of salt fish, and settles it within the hour by weighing the barrel herself; she writes it into her book as setting the pattern for every case after it.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Fèill Muileann òg first held

told_in.book: Of the Fair at Muileann òg
told_in.section: IV. Of the First Fair

events.title: The spoil-stone case judged by a smith's eye
events.body: A Cathair mhòr coal-carter brings a Sloc Mòr merchant's load of spoil-stone dressed to pass for coal-iron before Cùirt na Fèille; Oighrig nic Mhathain, having no forge of her own, sends the load to Muileann òg's one smith and fines the merchant by his judgment.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Fèill Muileann òg first held

told_in.book: Of the Fair at Muileann òg
told_in.section: IV. Of the First Fair

events.title: David Hale's wool turned away at the gate
events.body: David Hale of Caol mhòr brings four sacks of his father's wool to the fair's ninth day, the first cart from Tional nan Tuathach's own provinces to try it; Oighrig nic Mhathain reads him her own third clause and turns him to a factor's stall, where his wool sells for some fifth part less than a northern market would have given.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Oighrig nic Mhathain's rules

told_in.book: Of the Fair at Muileann òg
told_in.section: V. Of David Hale's Wool

events.title: The first fair runs a fortnight
events.body: The first fair at Muileann òg runs a fortnight, with wool from the western shires, An Sloc Mòr's coal from the east, Baile chiar's cloth and salt from the coastal pans on the one field, more trade than Oighrig nic Mhathain had seen gathered in nine years of market days.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Fèill Muileann òg first held

told_in.book: Of the Fair at Muileann òg
told_in.section: IV. Of the First Fair

events.title: Pipers from Baile chiar at the first fair
events.body: Pipers from Baile chiar play for coin at the far corner of the first fair's field, over the woodsmoke and wet wool and the coal carts' black dust, through the low constant argument of buying and selling in half a dozen tongues.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Fèill Muileann òg first held

told_in.book: Of the Fair at Muileann òg
told_in.section: IV. Of the First Fair

events.title: Dùn chrom's gate-toll
events.body: The toll taken at Dùn chrom's gate on the fair road pays for a new wall on the town's southern side. The townsfolk call it the fair's wall. The carters of the fair call it something else.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Dùn chrom's gate-toll raises the fair's wall

events.title: Niall dies; Brìghde crowned
events.body: Niall dies, and his daughter Brìghde follows him without contest: a mortal heir passing to a mortal heir among a nobility some of whom never age. It was thought no wonder then. It was thought one later.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The bells rung for Niall

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The council's oath sworn afresh

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The corrected proclamation at Ros dhomhain

events.title: The chronicler's use of the saying
events.body: Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill writes that the succession came 'mar a thàinig Niall'; it is the first time the saying is found in the royal record. In all her years as chronicler she lets no other idiom into the chronicle.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Gormshuil's struck drafts

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Gormshuil's resolve on the one idiom

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Gormshuil's mother laughs at the idiom

events.title: The ancestors' hall at Seann Dunn
events.body: The Seann Spioradan houses of the east coast build a common hall at Seann Dunn, where each year the living heads of forty families name their ancestors aloud. The next year the list is copied to the library, and it grows by a few names every year after.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The hall raised at Seann Dunn

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Gormshuil's visit to the first naming

links.label: Leads to
links.title: An Leabharlann's offer to Seann Dunn

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Nine generations named at Seann Dunn

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The Seann Dunn list first copied to an Leabharlann

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The fifth copy of the Seann Dunn naming

events.title: The fair's road metalled past Dùn chrom
events.body: In am Faoilleach the last stretch of the road from Cathair dhearg to Muileann òg is metalled for the fair's carts; the carters already call it Rathad na Fèille before the state gives it a name of its own.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The fair's road

told_in.book: Of the Fair at Muileann òg
told_in.section: VI. Of the Road, the Wall, and the Rule Read Aloud

events.title: Dùn chrom's gate-toll raises the fair's wall
events.body: The toll taken at Dùn chrom's gate on the fair's road pays, that same winter, for a new wall along the town's southern side, finished by an Cèitean; the townsfolk call it the fair's wall, and the carters call the gate by another name.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Dùn chrom's gate-toll

told_in.book: Of the Fair at Muileann òg
told_in.section: VI. Of the Road, the Wall, and the Rule Read Aloud

events.title: Tional nan Tuathach's letter against the factor rule filed
events.body: Walter Hale writes to the council on Tional nan Tuathach's behalf naming the factor rule a licence laid across a trade the north carried on unaided, and asks it looked at again; the council answers, months on, that the rule stands and will not be reconsidered inside the year, and the letter is filed with Tional nan Tuathach's earlier ones.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Oighrig nic Mhathain's rules

told_in.book: Of the Fair at Muileann òg
told_in.section: VI. Of the Road, the Wall, and the Rule Read Aloud

events.title: The fair's rules confirmed and read aloud
events.body: In an Lùnastal a council clerk reads Oighrig nic Mhathain's rules aloud before the gathered factors and maoir of the eastern shires, word for word as she wrote them, and asks whether the reading matches her own book; she tells him it does.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Oighrig nic Mhathain's rules

told_in.book: Of the Fair at Muileann òg
told_in.section: VI. Of the Road, the Wall, and the Rule Read Aloud

events.title: The bells rung for Niall
events.body: The bells of Òrd Mhacha at Cathair dhearg are rung a full day and a night for Niall's death, and the capital keeps no market. The crowd that gathers is the largest since his crowning; it stays quiet, and disperses before the second night.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Niall dies; Brìghde crowned

told_in.section: I. Of the Bells at Cathair dhearg

events.title: The council's oath sworn afresh
events.body: Comhairle na Rìoghachd, sitting on its fixed day within the week of the crowning, swears its oath of service afresh before Brìghde. The minute-book gives it one line among the day's ordinary business and no more.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Niall dies; Brìghde crowned

told_in.section: I. Of the Bells at Cathair dhearg

events.title: The corrected proclamation at Ros dhomhain
events.body: A harbour clerk at Ros dhomhain, copying the crowning's proclamation for the gate, writes Niall's name from habit, scores it through, and sets Brìghde's above the line. The corrected copy is kept under glass at the gate.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Niall dies; Brìghde crowned

told_in.section: I. Of the Bells at Cathair dhearg

events.title: Gormshuil's struck drafts
events.body: The chronicler writes and rejects three entries for the crowning before any stands: one too bare, one that says more than an office should say first, one left unfinished as an argument rather than a record. All three are struck through in her working book.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The chronicler's use of the saying

told_in.section: II. Of the Word Gormshuil Let In

events.title: Gormshuil's resolve on the one idiom
events.body: Having let *mar a thàinig Niall* into the royal record, the chronicler resolves to admit no other such phrase for as long as the office is hers, having seen other offices lose their plainness one borrowed ornament at a time.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The chronicler's use of the saying

told_in.section: II. Of the Word Gormshuil Let In

events.title: The hall raised at Seann Dunn
events.body: Forty households of Na Seann Spioradan along the east coast raise a common hall at Seann Dunn in a single season, working the stone by day, and roof it before the first frost. It holds no image or carving, only two hearths.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The ancestors' hall at Seann Dunn

told_in.section: III. Of the Hall at Seann Dunn

events.title: Gormshuil's visit to the first naming
events.body: The chronicler rides east to Seann Dunn to watch the hall's first naming of ancestors, not on an Leabharlann's business but her own, her mother's house keeping the same rite at a hearth too small for half its dead.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The ancestors' hall at Seann Dunn

told_in.section: III. Of the Hall at Seann Dunn

events.title: An Leabharlann's offer to Seann Dunn
events.body: Asked by an elder of the hall whether an Leabharlann keeps such lists of the dead, Gormshuil answers that it does not, but will keep any copy sent to it as carefully as anything else that reaches Muileann chaol.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The ancestors' hall at Seann Dunn

told_in.section: III. Of the Hall at Seann Dunn

events.title: The vote for a light at Cuan ruadh
events.body: After two boats are lost on the harbour rocks in a winter fog, the town council of Cuan ruadh votes its own coal money to burn a light on the mole where no board light has ever reached.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Cuan ruadh's harbour light

told_in.section: IV. Of the Light on the Mole

events.title: Gormshuil's mother laughs at the idiom
events.body: Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill's mother, hearing in her village by Ceann àrsaidh that her daughter has let mar a thàinig Niall into the royal record, laughs longer than Gormshuil thinks the thing deserves, and says her daughter spent years learning to write like nobody in particular so that she could in the end write like everybody.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The chronicler's use of the saying

told_in.section: II. Of the Word Gormshuil Let In

events.title: Nine generations named at Seann Dunn
events.body: At the first naming in the hall at Seann Dunn an old woman of the town recites nine generations of her dead before her voice gives out, and her son speaks the tenth for her.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The ancestors' hall at Seann Dunn

told_in.section: III. Of the Hall at Seann Dunn

events.title: Cuan ruadh's harbour light
events.body: Cuan ruadh on the east coast, which has none of the five lighthouses, raises a harbour light of its own on the mole and burns in it coal bought by the town. The Lighthouse Board will not take it on.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The vote for a light at Cuan ruadh

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Comhairle nan Taighean-solais's refusal

events.title: Còmhrag Ceann leathan first fought
events.body: A fierce melee is first fought at Ceann leathan, and is fought there every year after. It is held to be a martial custom. More and more it is where a people with few other outlets spend their anger.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The rules of the first Còmhrag

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The dead of the first Còmhrag buried

events.title: Calum Ruadh
events.body: The first champion of the Còmhrag whose name is remembered is Calum mac Aonghais, called Calum Ruadh, a hewer of Muileann chrom. Two men die in the melee he wins. The prize is a year's wages and the right to bear arms in any shire.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The dead of the first Còmhrag buried

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Calum Ruadh's purse counted out

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The right to bear arms entered on the shire's roll

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Calum Ruadh walks home alone

events.title: Ceann leathan's inns
events.body: Ceann leathan builds four new inns for the crowds of the Còmhrag. The fair-wardens of the town, who take a share of every room, become the Còmhrag's keepers in all but name.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The fair-wardens' free table

events.title: The Seann Dunn list first copied to an Leabharlann
events.body: The hall at Seann Dunn sends an Leabharlann the first copy of its naming, and goes on sending one every year after, each a little longer than the last. Gormshuil enters only the day it came and the count of names.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The ancestors' hall at Seann Dunn

told_in.section: III. Of the Hall at Seann Dunn

events.title: Comhairle nan Taighean-solais's refusal
events.body: The Comhairle nan Taighean-solais writes back to Cuan ruadh that its charter names five lights and no more, and that the town's own light, being no charge on An Crùn, may continue as it is. Gormshuil enters the refusal in four lines.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Cuan ruadh's harbour light

told_in.section: IV. Of the Light on the Mole

events.title: The rules of the first Còmhrag
events.body: The first Còmhrag at Ceann leathan is fought under rules that run to little more than a fee, a bar on edged weapons, and a purse for the last man standing inside the ropes. Nobody thinks the custom will need more than that.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Còmhrag Ceann leathan first fought

told_in.section: V. Of the Còmhrag

events.title: The dead of the first Còmhrag buried
events.body: Two men who do not walk out of the ropes at the first Còmhrag are buried at Ceann leathan within the week. Còmhrag Ceann leathan is fought again the following summer regardless, and the record gives their deaths one plain sentence.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Còmhrag Ceann leathan first fought

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Calum Ruadh

told_in.section: V. Of the Còmhrag

events.title: Calum Ruadh's purse counted out
events.body: A year's wages are counted out on a trestle table by the fair-wardens' own clerk for Calum mac Aonghais, hewer of Muileann chrom, who wins the first Còmhrag by refusing to stay down.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Calum Ruadh

told_in.section: V. Of the Còmhrag

events.title: The right to bear arms entered on the shire's roll
events.body: Calum Ruadh's right to bear arms in any shire of the kingdom, Còmhrag Ceann leathan's second prize, is entered that same evening on the shire's roll at Ceann leathan, a right his own father never held.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Calum Ruadh

told_in.section: V. Of the Còmhrag

events.title: The fair-wardens' free table
events.body: The inn-keepers of Ceann leathan, four of whom built new houses that year for Còmhrag Ceann leathan's crowds, keep Calum Ruadh's table free of charge, a custom nobody formally agrees to but that holds for as long as he comes back to fight.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Ceann leathan's inns

told_in.section: V. Of the Còmhrag

events.title: Calum Ruadh walks home alone
events.body: Calum Ruadh walks out of Ceann leathan before dawn the morning after the first Còmhrag with the purse in his coat and the shire clerk's paper folded inside it, past the shuttered inns and the field where the ropes were taken down in the night, and takes Rathad na Mèinne north toward Muileann chrom alone.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Calum Ruadh

told_in.section: V. Of the Còmhrag

events.title: The grain-ships of Ros gheal
events.body: Ros gheal on the north-central coast builds a dock for the grain-ships of the Hawk country. The Hawk houses bless the dock and ask a tithe of its dues. The shire gives them a twentieth.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Mary Coyle first speaks in Tional nan Tuathach

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The widows heard first

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Òrd an t-Seabhaig's twentieth first paid

events.title: Mary Coyle first speaks in Tional nan Tuathach
events.body: Mary Coyle, widowed of the Cuan bheag drowning, stands and speaks her own words in Tional nan Tuathach rather than sending a note forward to be read by another. The clerk David Hale sets her speech down whole in the day-book, the first time a woman's words are kept there entire rather than summed in a line.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The grain-ships of Ros gheal

told_in.section: II. Of Mary Coyle Standing Up

events.title: Splatter and Dodge's generation born
events.body: Many children are born in these years to the shunting families of the yard. From them come Seachran and Brean and others of that generation, who grow up to be Dubhan's closest allies.

events.title: Seann Bhral in the south
events.body: Seann Bhral on the south coast, not the town of that name in the west, becomes the greatest fishing port of the kingdom and lands more fish than Ros dhomhain. Its curing-sheds run the length of the harbour.

events.title: The widows heard first
events.body: Tional nan Tuathach resolves that the widows of the drowned be heard on the same footing as any man who has paid his shilling, and heard first when a matter touches their own dead. The rule is entered as standing, not as a courtesy for one night, on the widow Agnes Tulloch's motion.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The grain-ships of Ros gheal

told_in.section: II. Of Mary Coyle Standing Up

events.title: Òrd an t-Seabhaig's twentieth first paid
events.body: Ros gheal's factor pays Òrd an t-Seabhaig their first quarter's twentieth on the dues of the new grain dock, the sum the shire's factor haggled down from a tithe. The due is paid every quarter after, and the clerks of Ros gheal come to call it simply Òrd an t-Seabhaig's, few remembering why.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The grain-ships of Ros gheal

told_in.section: I. Of the Dock, the Twentieth, and the Names Given to Children

events.title: The circus at Seann Chwen
events.body: The travelling show that calls itself An Siorcas Siubhail Do-thuigsinn is first recorded, pitched near Seann Chwen on the southern coast. The chronicler's clerk could not say what its acts were meant to show. Nor, he adds, could the crowd, and it came back the next night.

events.title: Manannan's feast at Seann Bhral
events.body: The house of Òrd Mhanannain at Seann Bhral, one of the oldest on the west coast, will not admit the Tuathaich from the north who come to its feast of the sea, as their forebears learned to do from the Dia-thìrich harbours. Its keeper says the sea is the same and the house is not.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Tional nan Tuathach votes to send the western crossing

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Eleven boats sail for Seann Bhral

links.label: Leads to
links.title: A boat nearly lost off the passage

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The house at Seann Bhral answers Mary Coyle

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Mary Coyle resolves to keep the feast at Cnoc ghorm

links.label: Leads to
links.title: A Ros mhòr man asks what now

events.title: Tional nan Tuathach votes to send the western crossing
events.body: After two hard sittings Tional nan Tuathach agrees to Mary Coyle's asking, that northern boats sail west-about to keep the sea-feast at Seann Bhral where the Tuathaich forebears once kept it. Many in the room call it a fool's errand for winter, and are not silenced, only outvoted.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Manannan's feast at Seann Bhral

told_in.section: III. Of the Muster for Seann Bhral

events.title: Eleven boats sail for Seann Bhral
events.body: Eleven boats out of Caol mhòr, Cuan bheag and Ros mhòr put out on a grey morning at the end of an Lùnastal under Mary Coyle, carrying little but themselves, a keg of salt fish apiece, and Tional nan Tuathach's own sheet naming her their word. Ros bheag's harbour will not give them its quay, and sends them to a mooring buoy instead.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Manannan's feast at Seann Bhral

told_in.section: III. Of the Muster for Seann Bhral

events.title: A boat nearly lost off the passage
events.body: A squall out of the south-west puts green water over the bow of the smallest boat of the eleven, and its crew bails her clear with whatever will hold water. No one of the fleet is lost on the four days' passage, though more than one aboard call it the hardest going since An t-Aiseag itself.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Manannan's feast at Seann Bhral

told_in.section: III. Of the Muster for Seann Bhral

events.title: The house at Seann Bhral answers Mary Coyle
events.body: The keeper of Òrd Mhanannain at Seann Bhral in the west hears Mary Coyle's asking through to the end and refuses it: the house is kept on tithes of families who hold the rite by blood and the custodian's book, and cannot be opened on a four days' claim, however justly sailed. He tells her the sea is the same; the house is not.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Manannan's feast at Seann Bhral

told_in.section: IV. Of the House That Said the Sea Was the Same

events.title: Mary Coyle resolves to keep the feast at Cnoc ghorm
events.body: On the passage home Mary Coyle tells the crews the north will keep the feast of the sea itself, in full, at the church above Cnoc ghorm where a thin blessing of the boats is already kept each spring. The decision is made before the eleven boats raise Caol mhòr again.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Manannan's feast at Seann Bhral

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The northern sea-feast

told_in.section: V. Of the Feast They Made Their Own

events.title: A Ros mhòr man asks what now
events.body: On the third day home from Seann Bhral, off the northern capes, an old Ros mhòr hand who has said little the whole voyage asks Mary Coyle plainly what she means to do now that the west will not have them.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Manannan's feast at Seann Bhral

told_in.section: V. Of the Feast They Made Their Own

events.title: The northern sea-feast
events.body: Turned away at Seann Bhral, the Tuathaich keep the feast at the church at Cnoc ghorm instead, as a blessing of the boats. They keep it there every year after, and within a generation the northern feast is greater than the western.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Mary Coyle resolves to keep the feast at Cnoc ghorm

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The first Fleadh na Mara kept in full

links.label: Leads to
links.title: David Hale counts the boats at Cnoc ghorm

events.title: The first Fleadh na Mara kept in full
events.body: More than fifty boats gather at Cnoc ghorm on the second Sunday of an Gearran, far beyond any year before, and the parish priest blesses each hull in turn with heather dipped in harbour water. Mary Coyle's own boat, which carried her to Seann Bhral and back, is blessed fourth in the row.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The northern sea-feast

told_in.section: V. Of the Feast They Made Their Own

events.title: David Hale counts the boats at Cnoc ghorm
events.body: David Hale keeps a written count of the boats blessed at Cnoc ghorm for Tional nan Tuathach's day-book, the first such count taken of the feast. Word of the gathering's size travels the north coast faster than the crossing to Seann Bhral had, and boats are promised from as far as Inis mhin's country the year after.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The northern sea-feast

told_in.section: V. Of the Feast They Made Their Own

events.title: The Depletion first noted
events.body: The survey reports begin to note, without remark, that the vein yields less. For years the state does nothing.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Iain Mapa true up the eastern faces

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The vein found thinning east and south

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Comhairle nam Mèinnean's yield sent as a single figure

events.title: Iain Mapa's survey
events.body: The survey behind the report is the work of Iain mac Ruairidh, called Iain Mapa, of the Mine Board. His measures of the faces of the Sloc Mòr show the vein thinning to east and south. The Board files the survey and shows it to no one, and Iain Mapa is sent to the silver works at Muileann chiar.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Iain Mapa walks the survey to Cathair dhearg

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Comhairle nam Mèinnean leaves the survey unrolled

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Ruairidh mac Ailein signs the receipt

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The survey filed and shown to no one

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Iain Mapa posted to Muileann chiar

events.title: Iain Mapa true up the eastern faces
events.body: Sent into the eastern galleries of An Sloc Mòr to settle a dispute between two overseers over a cutting's bounds, the chainman Iain mac Ruairidh, called Iain Mapa, checks an old survey against the new digging and finds the figures will not lie flat. He walks the faces a second time before he trusts what they tell him.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The Depletion first noted

told_in.section: I. Of the Faces of the Sloc Mòr

events.title: The vein found thinning east and south
events.body: A third survey of the faces gives Iain Mapa the same figures as the first two, to within an inch the chain itself can account for: the vein runs narrower to the east than the old maps show, and pinches again to the south. He sets it down in a hand that does not shake, and does not argue.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The Depletion first noted

told_in.section: I. Of the Faces of the Sloc Mòr

events.title: Iain Mapa walks the survey to Cathair dhearg
events.body: Rather than trust the carters with a finding he believes Comhairle nam Mèinnean should see in his own hand, Iain Mapa rolls and ties his survey and walks the thirty-one miles from An Sloc Mòr to Cathair dhearg in a day and a half, sleeping one night on the road, and tells no one at the mine beforehand what the sheet holds.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Iain Mapa's survey

told_in.section: I. Of the Faces of the Sloc Mòr

events.title: Comhairle nam Mèinnean leaves the survey unrolled
events.body: Iain Mapa lays his survey before three men of Comhairle nam Mèinnean at Cathair dhearg and unties the string himself. None of the three unrolls it. He gives them the finding by mouth, plainly, and is told only, by the one in the middle, that it will be considered.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Iain Mapa's survey

told_in.section: II. Of the Receipt

events.title: Ruairidh mac Ailein signs the receipt
events.body: Asked for a receipt for the survey he has carried in, Iain Mapa is given four written lines naming nothing of the finding, only that a survey was received and filed. Ruairidh mac Ailein of Comhairle nam Mèinnean signs it, since the man in the middle will not, and Iain Mapa folds it into his pocket-book.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Iain Mapa's survey

told_in.section: II. Of the Receipt

events.title: The survey filed and shown to no one
events.body: Within the week Iain Mapa's survey is filed in Comhairle nam Mèinnean's own press at Cathair dhearg with the two years' surveys before it, and circulated to no one on the council or in any other office of the state. It lies there unread while the men who might have acted on it go on believing the mountain gives as freely as ever.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Iain Mapa's survey

told_in.section: III. Of the Rule Made at Cathair mhòr

events.title: Iain Mapa posted to Muileann chiar
events.body: Within the month Iain Mapa is told, with little explanation offered and none asked for, that he is wanted at the silver works at Muileann chiar, twenty-four miles east and a little south of An Sloc Mòr, where Comhairle nam Mèinnean has need of a man who holds a chain straight and asks no more than the work requires.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Iain Mapa's survey

told_in.section: II. Of the Receipt

events.title: Bàta an Achaidh warped into the new harbour
events.body: Of the hulls Tonn Mhòr Cnoc chaol cast into the fields behind Cuan dhearg two generations before, one is found sound enough to be dragged to the water, caulked and floated, and is warped into the rebuilt harbour ahead of every boat built new for it. The harbour-master keeps it moored at the quay-head as a relic rather than putting it back to work.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The harbour at Cuan dhearg reopened

told_in.section: V. Of the Boat Kept for a Relic

events.title: The Mine Board at Cathair mhòr
events.body: The Mine Board, which has sat at Cathair dhearg since the Sloc Mòr concession, moves its clerks to Cathair mhòr to be nearer the mountain. By the Board's own rule its surveys are kept there and not sent to the library.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Comhairle nam Mèinnean's clerks move to Cathair mhòr

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Riaghailt a' Bhùird set down

events.title: The scent-makers of Seann Vell
events.body: The glass-houses of the capital shore begin to make small flasks, and in them the women of Seann Vell sell the waters they distil from bog-myrtle, meadowsweet and heather honey. Within a few years scent is sold in every market town, and the towns of the western plain take up the trade.

events.title: The Grey Night forbidden
events.body: A Dia-thìreach magistrate at Baile chrom forbids the gatherings of the Grey Night sect as disorderly. Hannah Crane is fined. The vigil goes indoors and goes on.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Tional nan Tuathach pays Hannah Crane's fine

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Oidhche Glaise kept indoors

events.title: The harbour at Cuan dhearg reopened
events.body: The harbour at Cuan dhearg, lost to the Great Wave, is opened again with a new mole of dressed stone. The first boat in is one of those found in the fields behind the old town, refloated, and kept by the harbour-master as a relic.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Bàta an Achaidh warped into the new harbour

events.title: Comhairle nam Mèinnean's clerks move to Cathair mhòr
events.body: Comhairle nam Mèinnean moves its clerks and its presses the sixteen miles from Cathair dhearg to Cathair mhòr, into leased rooms above the town's wool market, on the stated ground that a board charged with the mountain's business ought to sit nearer the mountain than it had.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The Mine Board at Cathair mhòr

told_in.section: III. Of the Rule Made at Cathair mhòr

events.title: Riaghailt a' Bhùird set down
events.body: In four lines Comhairle nam Mèinnean sets down, for the first time in writing, the rule that its surveyors' work is to be kept at Cathair mhòr in Comhairle nam Mèinnean's own presses and not sent to Leabharlann Muileann chaol as every other office's reports are sent. No one on the council is asked to confirm it.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The Mine Board at Cathair mhòr

told_in.section: III. Of the Rule Made at Cathair mhòr

events.title: Tional nan Tuathach pays Hannah Crane's fine
events.body: Word reaches Tional nan Tuathach that the vigil-keeper Hannah Crane has been fined at Baile chrom for keeping Oidhche Glaise in the open. Tional nan Tuathach votes the balance of her fine out of its own small chest without much debate, on a councillor's motion that a woman fined for standing on a beach is no threat worth agreeing with.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The Grey Night forbidden

told_in.section: IV. Of Small Trades and a Forbidden Night

events.title: Oidhche Glaise kept indoors
events.body: Forbidden the open shingle below the light, Oidhche Glaise is kept that year in a byre lent by a family who hold the old rite themselves, one night a year, in a silence the magistrate's order cannot reach any better than it reached the shore. Outsiders are still not told which night it falls on.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The Grey Night forbidden

told_in.section: IV. Of Small Trades and a Forbidden Night

events.title: Achadh mhin's old bounds restored
events.body: The shire measures the returning households of Achadh mhin back onto the same strips the humans' surveyors once cut, the old plat being the one the families still walk by memory rather than a new line drawn by a Dia-thìreach chain.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Achadh mhin resettled

told_in.section: I. Of Achadh mhin's Fields

events.title: Achadh mhin resettled
events.body: The fields of Achadh mhin bear again, and a few of the families moved away after the Great Wave come back to them. The shire gives them their old bounds from the humans' survey.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Achadh mhin's old bounds restored

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Idle looms at Baile chiar

links.label: Leads to
links.title: A wedding at Lia Fàil's door in Doire shean

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The first households return to Achadh mhin

events.title: Idle looms at Baile chiar
events.body: The weavers' guild of Baile chiar reports the washing-pools behind its fulling-sheds too low after a dry summer to scour wool, and its looms idle three weeks; the guild counts the bolts not woven to the last half-ell and does not count the weavers it has not paid.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Achadh mhin resettled

told_in.section: IV. Of the Ordinary Traffic

events.title: A wedding at Lia Fàil's door in Doire shean
events.body: The harbour-master of Doire shean writes to an Leabharlann of his daughter's wedding to a clerk of Lia Fàil's counting-room, kept at Lia Fàil's door, the first in his memory for which the whole fishing fleet came in on one tide to stand on the quay.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Achadh mhin resettled

told_in.section: IV. Of the Ordinary Traffic

events.title: Eòghan crowned
events.body: Brìghde dies young, and no cause is made known. Her cousin Eòghan takes the throne, and for the first time the restored kingdom's succession is in dispute.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The twice-sealed packet reaches Muileann chaol

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Gormshuil's three struck drafts

events.title: The succession entry
events.body: The royal chronicler's entry for the succession gives the bare fact. The chroniclers after Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill have added nothing to it.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Gormshuil's three struck drafts

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The bare entry set down

events.title: Dissent recorded in council
events.body: For the first time the council's minutes record votes against a succession. They name the councillors who voted, and not their reasons. Two of them do not sit again.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The council's four lines on the division

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Tormod mac Iain Òig goes home

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Sìleas nic Artair keeps her own house's rite

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The council's two seats filled

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Leabhar nam Breith cited by its page

events.title: The first households return to Achadh mhin
events.body: Three households moved off the salted fields after Tonn Mhòr Cnoc chaol, or their children in their place, ask and are granted their old ground back, the barley coming up along strips long thought lost to the tide.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Achadh mhin resettled

told_in.section: I. Of Achadh mhin's Fields

events.title: The twice-sealed packet reaches Muileann chaol
events.body: Word of Brìghde's death and Eòghan's crowning reaches the chronicler's desk in a packet sealed twice, the second hand adding, in a hastier line at the foot, that the council's own sitting on the succession did not pass as quietly as the crowning itself.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Eòghan crowned

told_in.section: II. Of the Bare Entry

events.title: Gormshuil's three struck drafts
events.body: The chronicler writes and rejects three entries for the succession before a fourth stands: one that says more than an office should say first, one so bare it reads as a door shut on purpose, one left unfinished as an argument rather than a record.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Eòghan crowned

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The succession entry

told_in.section: II. Of the Bare Entry

events.title: The bare entry set down
events.body: Past the second hour of the morning Gormshuil enters the day of Brìghde's death, the fact that no cause is made known, and the day of Eòghan's crowning, and nothing more, choosing the silence rather than dressing it as a fullness it is not.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The succession entry

told_in.section: II. Of the Bare Entry

events.title: The council's four lines on the division
events.body: The council's own minute of the sitting names Tormod mac Iain Òig and Sìleas nic Artair as the two who stood against seating Eòghan, gives no reason either offered, and closes with the plainest of its four lines: the two do not sit again.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Dissent recorded in council

told_in.section: III. Of the Votes Recorded

events.title: Tormod mac Iain Òig goes home
events.body: Tormod mac Iain Òig returns to his own lands in the western shires and is not named in Eachdraidh na Rìoghachd again for some years, his seat on the council closed behind him without further entry.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Dissent recorded in council

told_in.section: III. Of the Votes Recorded

events.title: Sìleas nic Artair keeps her own house's rite
events.body: Sìleas nic Artair, her council seat lost with Tormod mac Iain Òig's, gives her Na Seann Spioradan kin's house more of her time than council business ever left her, and does not sit at Cathair dhearg again.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Dissent recorded in council

told_in.section: III. Of the Votes Recorded

events.title: The council's two seats filled
events.body: Before the year turns the council seats a landed man's son from the western shires and a widow of a coastal house in the two empty places, and neither newcomer is asked in council to account for the vote that opened the seat they now hold.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Dissent recorded in council

told_in.section: III. Of the Votes Recorded

events.title: Leabhar nam Breith cited by its page
events.body: Riding his twelfth year on the northern circuit, Uilleam mac Leòid finds for a Tuathaich family's grazing claim at Àth àrsaidh in the words of his aunt's ruling and cites Leabhar nam Breith by its page, the first circuit return to cite the book in its own words.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Dissent recorded in council

told_in.section: IV. Of the Ordinary Traffic

events.title: Comhairle nam Mèinnean's yield sent as a single figure
events.body: Comhairle nam Mèinnean's return to Eachdraidh na Rìoghachd gives An Sloc Mòr's yield for the year as a single figure, no faces named and no survey cited; Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill enters it and sets the year before's figure beside it in her smallest hand, with no word between them.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The Depletion first noted

told_in.section: IV. Of the Ordinary Traffic

events.title: The fifth copy of the Seann Dunn naming
events.body: The hall at Seann Dunn sends an Leabharlann its fifth copy of the naming, longer by eleven names, the hall having taken in three households of the coast that had kept their dead at their own hearths until then.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The ancestors' hall at Seann Dunn

told_in.section: IV. Of the Ordinary Traffic

events.title: The warehouse quarter of Inis bhàn burns two days
events.body: Fire takes three storehouses and the dwellings above them at Inis bhàn on the Abhainn ìseal and burns two days before the town beats it back street by street with buckets and wet sacking; every soul in the burning quarter gets clear, and none dies.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Inis bhàn's fire

told_in.section: V. Of the Fire at Inis bhàn and the Letter of the Schools

events.title: Inis bhàn's fire
events.body: Fire takes the warehouse quarter of Inis bhàn on the Abhainn ìseal in the north-central country and burns for two days. The town's Hawk house takes in the homeless. The fire-bell the town buys afterwards is the loudest in the kingdom.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The warehouse quarter of Inis bhàn burns two days

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Òrd an t-Seabhaig house at Inis bhàn opens its doors

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Inis bhàn's new bell rung on the quay

events.title: Dubhan born
events.body: Dubhan is born mortal, in the north where the Severance confined his people, decades after the war that shut the island against those from whom his line descends.

events.title: The Tuathaich schools counted
events.body: The Moot counts eleven schools in the north that teach in the humans' tongue, and three that have begun to teach Dia-thìris as well, at the parents' asking. Agnes Pike's school at Doire ghlas is one of the three.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Tional nan Tuathach's letter of the eleven schools

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Three schools begin teaching Dia-thìris

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Agnes Pike's school teaches its first Dia-thìris lesson

events.title: Òrd an t-Seabhaig house at Inis bhàn opens its doors
events.body: Òrd an t-Seabhaig house at Inis bhàn, which has never before taken in households outside those sworn to it, shelters every family the fire puts out of a roof, sworn or not, through the worst of the spring cold.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Inis bhàn's fire

told_in.section: V. Of the Fire at Inis bhàn and the Letter of the Schools

events.title: Inis bhàn's new bell rung on the quay
events.body: Inis bhàn buys a bell from the founders' yard at Cathair dhearg, cast to the town's own order, to stand where the old warehouse bell burned, rung once on the quay before it is hung, and heard, by the town's own telling, further up and down the Abhainn ìseal than any bell in the kingdom.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Inis bhàn's fire

told_in.section: V. Of the Fire at Inis bhàn and the Letter of the Schools

events.title: Tional nan Tuathach's letter of the eleven schools
events.body: Walter Hale writes Tional nan Tuathach's count of the north's schools to Muileann chaol, eleven in all from Agnes Pike's byre at Doire ghlas to a room over a chandler's shop at Ceann àrsaidh opened that same autumn, and Gormshuil enters it whole rather than shortened.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The Tuathaich schools counted

told_in.section: V. Of the Fire at Inis bhàn and the Letter of the Schools

events.title: Three schools begin teaching Dia-thìris
events.body: At three of the north's eleven schools the teachers begin, at the parents' own asking and with no order from the council or leave from any maor, to teach Dia-thìris alongside the humans' letters, so that children may read a proclamation or a boundary-line in the tongue the kingdom writes its business in.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The Tuathaich schools counted

told_in.section: V. Of the Fire at Inis bhàn and the Letter of the Schools

events.title: Agnes Pike's school teaches its first Dia-thìris lesson
events.body: Agnes Pike's school at Doire ghlas, one of the three Tional nan Tuathach's letter names, sets its first Dia-thìris lesson beside am Bìoball and Tional nan Tuathach's own minutes, at the asking of the parents whose children it has taught since its founding.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The Tuathaich schools counted

told_in.section: V. Of the Fire at Inis bhàn and the Letter of the Schools

events.title: The stone house of Mac Ùisdein
events.body: Uisdean mac Ùisdein's house at Cathair mhòr is rebuilt in stone quarried from the spoil of the Sloc Mòr, the greatest private house in the kingdom. The Guild of Hewers holds its feast in the new hall.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Comann nan Gualadairean feasts in the new hall

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The mason's letter of the hall he did not sit in

events.title: Comann nan Gualadairean feasts in the new hall
events.body: Comann nan Gualadairean holds its feast in the finished stone hall of Uisdean mac Ùisdein at Cathair mhòr, at tables set the length of the room under torches an ironsmith made to no pattern but his own, and Mòrag nic Coinnich attends as an Leabharlann's own witness.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The stone house of Mac Ùisdein

told_in.section: I. Of the New Hall at Cathair mhòr

events.title: The northern fishing grounds
events.body: Licences to fish the waters south and east of Caol mhòr are kept for Dia-thìrich boats. The Tuathaich boats are left the northern grounds, where the raiders also fish.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The first licence refused to a Caol mhòr boat

events.title: Doire shean's harbour
events.body: Doire shean in the south-west builds a stone harbour for the fishing boats of the Stone's country, the first new harbour since the Severance not paid for by the Crown. The house of the Stone lends the money and takes the harbour dues.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The house of Lia Fàil takes its first quarter's dues

events.title: The mason's letter of the hall he did not sit in
events.body: A mason who dressed the stone of Mac Ùisdein's new hall writes an Leabharlann that he was not asked to the guild's own feast in it, his craft holding no sworn place for a cutter of stone, and Ailean Leabhar enters the letter whole rather than in his own shorter hand.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The stone house of Mac Ùisdein

told_in.section: I. Of the New Hall at Cathair mhòr

events.title: The first licence refused to a Caol mhòr boat
events.body: Sam Ridley, a Tuathaich master who has fished the southern banks off Caol mhòr eleven years, brings his catch to the maor's scales the day the new licences take force and is told the grounds are not, at present, being papered for boats of his fleet; Tional nan Tuathach enters the day and his name.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The northern fishing grounds

told_in.section: I. Of the New Hall at Cathair mhòr

events.title: The house of Lia Fàil takes its first quarter's dues
events.body: The house of Lia Fàil at Doire shean takes its first quarter's harbour dues off the new quay before the mole's last course is dry, the sum entered beside what the house first lent the town for the building of it.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Doire shean's harbour

told_in.section: I. Of the New Hall at Cathair mhòr

events.title: Trenches at Làrach an Dùin
events.body: Diggers sent by the library open trenches at Làrach an Dùin on the south-east coast. They find walls older than any Dia-thìreach building, and no writing at all. Ailean Leabhar has the finds entered as of the Old Ones, purpose unknown.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The diggers' camp opens at Làrach an Dùin

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Ailean Leabhar rides to the trenches

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The finds laid in an Leabharlann

events.title: Beathag asks that the temple's ground be left
events.body: Beathag, eldest of three Seann Spioradan elders of the district, meets Ailean Leabhar at Làrach an Teampaill and asks that an Leabharlann measure the ruin rather than open it, since whatever lies under the stone is neither hers to claim nor his.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Làrach an Teampaill measured

told_in.section: III. Of Làrach an Teampaill

events.title: Làrach an Teampaill measured
events.body: The library's diggers measure the ruin called Làrach an Teampaill in the east and do not dig it, at the asking of the Seann Spioradan houses of the district. The keeper enters it as measured and let be.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Beathag asks that the temple's ground be left

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The finds laid in an Leabharlann

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Ailean measures the temple with a chain, not a spade

events.title: The diggers' camp opens at Làrach an Dùin
events.body: Four diggers under a foreman named Cailean cut trenches through the spring above the headland at Làrach an Dùin, following the line of a coursed wall sunk deeper than any footing they have found the bottom of.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Trenches at Làrach an Dùin

told_in.section: II. Of the Trenches at Làrach an Dùin

events.title: Ailean Leabhar rides to the trenches
events.body: Neach-gleidhidh an Leabharlainn goes down himself to Làrach an Dùin on the diggers' word that the wall they have found is older than any ruin an Leabharlann holds a record of, and spends four days at the trench's edge with a lamp and a notebook.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Trenches at Làrach an Dùin

told_in.section: II. Of the Trenches at Làrach an Dùin

events.title: The finds laid in an Leabharlann
events.body: Ailean Leabhar carries the season's three findings, the wall's short entry, the measure of Làrach an Teampaill, and the copied obelisk, into an Leabharlann's own presses himself, filing the not-knowing of each as carefully as a certainty.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Trenches at Làrach an Dùin

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Làrach an Teampaill measured

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The obelisk at Cnoc bheag copied

told_in.section: VI. Of the Salt-Pans and the New Deputy

events.title: Ailean measures the temple with a chain, not a spade
events.body: Ailean Leabhar spends two days at Làrach an Teampaill setting down the line of the fallen wall and the fall of the ground with a chain and a level, and enters the ruin as measured, and let be.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Làrach an Teampaill measured

told_in.section: III. Of Làrach an Teampaill

events.title: Una copies Carragh Cnoc bheag stroke by stroke
events.body: Una, a scribe trained under Ailean Leabhar in copying an Leabharlann's most damaged leaves, spends three weeks of fair days at the foot of Carragh Cnoc bheag setting down every stroke of its unread script exactly as the stone gives it, worn gap for worn gap.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The obelisk at Cnoc bheag copied

told_in.section: IV. Of the Obelisk at Cnoc bheag

events.title: The council pays for a fence at Carragh Cnoc bheag
events.body: On the keeper's word that a stone unread for longer than the kingdom's whole span deserves at least a fence against the cattle, the council finds the money for four posts and a rail set well back from Carragh Cnoc bheag's foot.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The obelisk at Cnoc bheag copied

told_in.section: IV. Of the Obelisk at Cnoc bheag

events.title: The obelisk at Cnoc bheag copied
events.body: A scribe of the library copies the writing on the obelisk near Cnoc bheag, stroke by stroke. It is like no script known on the island. The copy is filed and the obelisk fenced.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The finds laid in an Leabharlann

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Una copies Carragh Cnoc bheag stroke by stroke

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The council pays for a fence at Carragh Cnoc bheag

events.title: The keeper of Baile chrom's lighthouse reports the vigil
events.body: A Dia-thìrich keeper new to the lighthouse at Baile chrom reports Oidhche Glaise sect's yearly vigil kept silent in the tower's own shadow, and makes no move against it, having no order that names a silent watch on open ground his business.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: A lighthouse on the Tuathaich coast

told_in.section: V. Of the Lighthouse's Shadow

events.title: A lighthouse on the Tuathaich coast
events.body: The Dia-thìreach keeper of Taigh-solais Baile chrom reports to the council that the Grey Night sect keeps its vigil in the dark of the lighthouse's own shadow. The council does nothing.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The keeper of Baile chrom's lighthouse reports the vigil

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The council answers the keeper's report with nothing

events.title: Salt-pans of Àth bheag
events.body: Salt-pans are dug on the flats below Àth bheag on the east coast, and within a few years the town supplies the whole eastern seaboard. The salt goes inland by the old drove road past Baile ìseal.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: A salt-master of Àth bheag buys a lorry

links.label: Legacy of
links.title: The last ox-drove on the eastern salt road

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Mòrag nic Coinnich made Ailean's deputy

events.title: The council answers the keeper's report with nothing
events.body: No order reaches the keeper of Baile chrom's lighthouse, and no word reaches the magistrate who had once fined the vigil in the open, and Ailean Leabhar enters the council's silence into an Leabharlann's register as plainly as any finding.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: A lighthouse on the Tuathaich coast

told_in.section: V. Of the Lighthouse's Shadow

events.title: Mòrag nic Coinnich made Ailean's deputy
events.body: On the road home from Àth bheag, Ailean Leabhar asks Mòrag nic Coinnich to stand as an Leabharlann's deputy after a season that has taught him one keeper alone is a Library one bad season from having nobody who can speak for it; she agrees, on the condition that the register always name her deputy and never keeper.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Salt-pans of Àth bheag

told_in.section: VI. Of the Salt-Pans and the New Deputy

events.title: Cathair fhada's grain-store
events.body: Cathair fhada on the southern plain builds a Crown grain-store great enough to feed the south for a season. It is filled from the south's own harvests, and first opened in the dry years at Achadh shean.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The grain-store at Cathair fhada opens its doors

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The masons sign the grain-store's mortar

events.title: The grain-store at Cathair fhada opens its doors
events.body: In the dry weeks of a poor season the keeper of the new Crown grain-store walks out to the road and tells the first cart that passes that the south will eat that year whatever the sky withholds, and word of the opened doors outruns, by an evening, word of how bad the year will prove.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Cathair fhada's grain-store

told_in.section: I. Of the Grain-Store at Cathair fhada

events.title: The second census after the Severance
events.body: The second census measures for the first time how far the Tuathaich live below the Dia-thìrich; until now it was only seen. The report is not made public.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The second census rides the shire roads

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The council locks the second census away

events.title: Walter Hale dies
events.body: Walter Hale, first speaker of the Moot, dies at Caol mhòr. The Moot chooses Mary Coyle, a fisherman's widow, to follow him, the first woman to hold the chair.

links.label: Caused by
links.title: Peter Hale carries the books to Doire ghlas

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Walter Hale settles a carter's toll dispute

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Walter Hale dies at Caol mhòr

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The north walks to Hale's burial

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Tional nan Tuathach names Mary Coyle speaker

links.label: Leads to
links.title: David Hale keeps the books under Mary Coyle

events.title: The second census rides the shire roads
events.body: Clerks sent out a second time from Cathair dhearg tally hearth against hearth as before, but with a new column set beside the first, a figure for what a Dia-thìreach household holds and one for what its Tuathach neighbour holds, so that the count for once measures the gap rather than only setting the numbers side by side.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The second census after the Severance

told_in.section: I. Of the Grain-Store at Cathair fhada

events.title: The council locks the second census away
events.body: The sums the shire clerks carry back to Cathair dhearg go onto a stack in the council's own keeping-room and no further; no proclamation, no minute copied to an Leabharlann, no word to any shire clerk who might have carried it on, and the twelve who asked for the count give out only that the figures want study before they want airing.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The second census after the Severance

told_in.section: I. Of the Grain-Store at Cathair fhada

events.title: Walter Hale settles a carter's toll dispute
events.body: Keeping the thirty-year habit of hearing the furthest-travelled petitioner before the day's set business, Walter Hale hears out a carter from beyond Àth fhada over a wrongly charged toll and settles it in the carter's favour himself, his voice unhurried though the sitting leaves him more spent than harder business had the winter before.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Walter Hale dies

told_in.section: II. Of Walter Hale's Last Sittings

events.title: Walter Hale dies at Caol mhòr
events.body: Walter Hale, first speaker of Tional nan Tuathach, dies in his own bed at Caol mhòr on the twenty-eighth of an Gearran, seventy-six years old, David beside him and Alice sent for but not in time; Tional nan Tuathach's business stops three days without a vote taken to stop it.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Walter Hale dies

told_in.section: III. Of the Twenty-Eighth of an Gearran

events.title: The north walks to Hale's burial
events.body: Fishermen, carters and shepherds from every part of the north crowd the roads into Caol mhòr for Walter Hale's burial, more feet on the road that week than the fair itself drew the autumn before, and he is laid in sight of Tional nan Tuathach's own house where he sat thirty-one years.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Walter Hale dies

told_in.section: III. Of the Twenty-Eighth of an Gearran

events.title: Tional nan Tuathach names Mary Coyle speaker
events.body: On the fourth day after Hale's burial Tional nan Tuathach sets aside a factor's son and a shire clerk both spoken for the chair and names Mary Coyle, a fisherman's widow of Caol mhòr, the first woman to hold it, by a count nobody in the room troubles to call close.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Walter Hale dies

told_in.section: III. Of the Twenty-Eighth of an Gearran

events.title: David Hale keeps the books under Mary Coyle
events.body: David Hale, who kept his father's minute-books through the years of the first fair, sets Mary Coyle's seal at her own place beside the one his father's hand had set to thirty-one years of letters, and stays on at her asking to keep the rough book as he always has.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Walter Hale dies

told_in.section: III. Of the Twenty-Eighth of an Gearran

events.title: Seonag nic Ille-Mhoire asks to see the report
events.body: Seonag nic Ille-Mhoire, who rode her own shire's tally in for the second census, asks a council clerk at Cathair dhearg to let her see the island's whole sum, on the ground that she carried the figures herself and has a right to know their total.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The census clerks' private note

told_in.section: IV. Of the Report Asked For and Refused

events.title: Seonag writes the refusal into her own book
events.body: Refused the report with no reason beyond the plain fact of the refusal, Seonag nic Ille-Mhoire writes the asking and the answer that same evening into a private book she keeps for herself and shows to no one, for a record's own sake rather than any purpose she could name.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The census clerks' private note

told_in.section: IV. Of the Report Asked For and Refused

events.title: Ruth Ashby and Clara Tulloch begin under Eachann mac Rath
events.body: Two women of the shunting country north of Caol mhòr, Ruth Ashby and Clara Tulloch, come to the surgery of Eachann mac Rath at Àth àrsaidh, who takes them without his guild's leave to be taught by watching him set bones and mix poultices through a hard, fever-crowded season.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The Tuathaich doctors

told_in.section: V. Of the Doctors of Àth àrsaidh

events.title: The guild's men find Eachann's surgery out
events.body: Word from a factor's wife reaches the physicians' guild that Eachann mac Rath's two new pupils handle a lancet as steady as he does, and two of the guild's own men ride to Àth àrsaidh and watch Ruth Ashby set a child's wrist unwatched before they leave without a word to either woman.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The Tuathaich doctors

told_in.section: V. Of the Doctors of Àth àrsaidh

events.title: Eachann mac Rath struck from the physicians' guild
events.body: The guild strikes Eachann mac Rath from its rolls before an Cèitean is out, its letter naming no fault in his physic, only that he taught outside its leave and to hands its charter does not recognise, and he sets the letter aside and keeps his surgery open all the same.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The Tuathaich doctors

told_in.section: V. Of the Doctors of Àth àrsaidh

events.title: The masons sign the grain-store's mortar
events.body: When the last course goes onto An Crùn's grain-store at Cathair fhada in the dry season, two winters building and one summer roofing, the masons sign their names in the mortar.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Cathair fhada's grain-store

told_in.section: I. Of the Grain-Store at Cathair fhada

events.title: The census clerks' private note
events.body: Seonag nic Ille-Mhoire, one of the census clerks, leaves among her papers a note that she asked to see the report on the gap and was refused. The note came to the library with her papers after her death. It is the only mention of the report outside the council.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Seonag nic Ille-Mhoire asks to see the report

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Seonag writes the refusal into her own book

events.title: The Tuathaich doctors
events.body: The Moot pays for two Tuathaich women to be taught medicine by a Dia-thìreach physician at Àth àrsaidh, who takes them against the will of his guild. He is struck from its rolls. They practise in the north for forty years.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Ruth Ashby and Clara Tulloch begin under Eachann mac Rath

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The guild's men find Eachann's surgery out

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Eachann mac Rath struck from the physicians' guild

events.title: The Abhainn ìseal takes three bridges and the embankment
events.body: Three days of hard rain in am Màrt bring the Abhainn ìseal over its lower banks, and the flood carries away three bridges and a long stretch of Slighe a' Ghuail's embankment, a carter losing his cart on the middle span but no soul drowned along that reach.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The Abhainn ìseal floods

told_in.section: VI. Of the Flood on the Abhainn ìseal

events.title: The Abhainn ìseal floods
events.body: The Abhainn ìseal, longest river of the island, breaks its banks along its lower reach and carries away three bridges and a stretch of the coal line's embankment. The line is shut most of a year, and the ports live on stored coal.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The Abhainn ìseal takes three bridges and the embankment

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Slighe a' Ghuail shuts and the ports live on stored coal

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Mary Coyle gives her first order as speaker

links.label: Leads to
links.title: David Hale keeps no second copy

events.title: Slighe a' Ghuail shuts and the ports live on stored coal
events.body: With a mile of embankment gone under the Abhainn ìseal's flood Slighe a' Ghuail shuts for want of ground to run on, and the ports that lived on what it carried, Ros dhomhain and the western harbours among them, turn to whatever coal they had laid by against a leaner week rather than a whole season.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The Abhainn ìseal floods

told_in.section: VI. Of the Flood on the Abhainn ìseal

events.title: Mary Coyle gives her first order as speaker
events.body: Not yet a month in the chair, Mary Coyle calls Tional nan Tuathach together the evening word of the washed embankment reaches Caol mhòr and orders every northern harbour that answers to Tional nan Tuathach to open its own coal store and share it out by the count of hearths rather than by whoever reaches the yard first, until the line can be walked and mended.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The Abhainn ìseal floods

told_in.section: VI. Of the Flood on the Abhainn ìseal

events.title: David Hale keeps no second copy
events.body: On the night Mary Coyle gives her first order as speaker, David Hale writes it into the rough book under her name and, for the first time in two years, keeps no second copy of the day's minute by his own hearth.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The Abhainn ìseal floods

told_in.section: III. Of the Twenty-Eighth of an Gearran

events.title: The Hawk houses' own custodian
